div.head: Prologue
div.p: I can tell even from here, most noble ladies, that you are amazed to see me here before you in these clothes and amid this scenery, as if we were about to present some comedy to you. You must not have expected a comedy, for up until last year, as you may be aware, the Intronati were concerned with other things. Then the other day you found out how they felt about you and learned that they no longer want to be bitten, chewed, and cut to the quick by you. So, as you saw, they burned those things that were capable of arousing their fantasies and increasing their desire for you as well as for your beauties. Now I want to make you forget all those strange things. There Intronati, to tell you the truth (and you can believe me, because I heard then say it), are very sorry to have become involved in such madness and are scared stiff that you (being quite capable of it) will have taken their hard points so deeply to heart that in the future you will withhold your tongues from them and turn your backs on them every time you see them. That’s why they’ve shoved me out here as their ambassador, orator, legate, lawyer, or poet, hoping that you’ll stick the matter, in whatever way it enters best, into the very backside of your memory. I find that I come before you [looking at his crotch] with a large mandate, in good shape. So have faith in me, or I’ll be forced to show it to you, as long as I’ve brought it along. I tell you that I’m here specifically to make this peace with you and to get you back together with them, if you are willing; for to tell you the truth, their affairs have gone cold and flaccid without you and have almost faded away, and if you don’t make it up with them, they will dwindle away to nothing. Hey, do it! Do it, ladies, it will give only pleasure. After all, you know how they are: if you look at them even once with a little pity, they’ll let you control them, they’ll be putty in your hands (but only for you, because with others they wouldn’t be so capable), and they’ll let you sweetly torture them, touch their, um, hearts with your words, always be on top and always come first. Well, what do you think? Are you content? Will you do it? You’re not responding. But then you aren’t refusing either, which is a good sign. Look, they were so eager to make this peace that they’ve put this comedy together in barely three days, and today they want you to see and hear it, if you are willing. Now you understand what this scene is doing here, who I am, and what I'm here to do for you. This comedy, from what I've heard, they call The Deceived, not because they were ever deceived by you. Oh, no! You have never tricked them - they know you all too well for that; rather, you have always compelled them, for they simply couldn't ever resist you. So they call the comedy this because almost all of the characters involved are deceived. Still, dear ladies, for all the ill will in which I hold you, there are some deceptions here that, God willing, I would be glad to play on you if you were the victims and I was the trickster, and to tell the truth I wouldn't even care if you turned the tables and got on top of me. The story is new and not taken form any source outside of their fevered brains - the same place where on the night of the Befana they decided your fate in such a way as to make you think that the Intronati were wronging you with what they said and that they have evil tongues. If you were to taste their tongues, perhaps you wouldn't feel that way but would defend them instead and take their parts as good companions wherever necessary. I am well aware that there are plenty of people who will say that this comedy is just a grab bag. To them I make no reply, because however things turn out, it's enough if you enjoy, for the Intronati have always addressed themselves to giving pleasure above all else. And they think it will be easy for them to do this for you ladies, especially those of you who are pregnant, who normally prefer ground-up coal, thread tea, brick dust, and the like to comedies. As far as the men in the audience are concerned, we really don't care whether they like it or not, because the Intronati have ordered that none of them may see or hear this unless they're already blind. Still, of there's some stuck-up scumbag of a man, drawn by an uncontrolled urge to criticize us, who is here and who really wishes to see and hear it, he'll have to cut out his eyes if he wants to understand it. I imagine you think it's strange that only blind men should watch this comedy. But it's true, and if you just have a little patience you'll understand, for I'll show you why. Whatever, beauty there is in the world today is without doubt here in Siena, and whatever beauty there is in Siena is present in this hall. This cannot be denied, because I can't believe that those who aren't here could be as beautiful as you or even close, since they stay away rather than be compared with you. How do you imagine men could come here to marvel at scenes or comedies, or to listen to or watch what we do or say, with you beautiful women here before them? What more beautiful game, what more beautiful spectacle, what more pleasing or beautiful thing could a man see than you ladies? Nothing, certainly. So now I have shown you why men may not see or hear this comedy unless they are blind, and you see I'm not quite as full of it as you thought. But you ladies will see and hear it just fine, because we know you well enough indeed to know that you're too well mannered ever to get carried away or lose self-control from looking at our beauty. Nor should those males who try so hard to be pretty - all dressed up, all shaved, who think they're so sophisticated because they have a well-kept beard, wear good boots, and know how to bow with their hat in hand and sign loud enough to be heard all the way to the Becci fountain - think that you will ignore our comedy in order to pay attention to them. If they think that, they will be the deceived and this will steal the name of our comedy. Now, it's possible that you'll see a Spaniard in our comedy whose strange talk will ruin your pleasure a bit and make it hard to follow our plot. But let me give you a good tip: don't pay any attention to him, for you don't speak his language and you won't be able to follow what he says; instead, give your attention to what the Italians say, and everything will be fine. But you know, I see some men over there watching you so intently that they haven't heard a thing I've said, so I might as well speak to you frankly and intimately for a second. It is possible, then, seeing how ungrateful you are, that these Intronati will always need to complain about you and return to this subject over and over again and in every place? And all the suffering they have endured for you and all the work they have put into praising you - has this still not been able to move you to grant them a bit of pleasure? Oh, in God's name, ease up a bit and call them to you one at time and try to listen to what they have to say and what they want from you. I'm absolutely sure that what they want is only a trifle, and you're so rich in it that it would cost you nothing to give it to them, and in fact to give it to the whole city as well. Tell me, honestly, what do you think they really want? They aren't looking for anything from you beyond your graces, and when you come to know their penetrating wit - whether it be large or small - you can say "I like this" or "I don't like this" so that those who don't appeal to you can turn their wit elsewhere and work on penetrating other subjects. But it's a serious matter that you insist on keeping them in this constant dither and won't ever resolve matters by using that blessed word "yes." Do you understand what I'm trying to say? Watch out that you don't make them genuinely give up in despair, and remember my words, because I know just what I'm talking about. Eventually you'll lose them for good, and then there will be no way to get them back, and you'll be sorry when it's too late. And you can be sure of this: that there are other options. Enough. Now that I think about it, don't expect any explanation of the plot, because the person who was supposed to do it isn't up to it. For now you can do without an explanation. It's enough that you know that this city behind me is Modena this year, and that the people who appear in this story are for the most part from that city. But if they make some mistakes with the dialect of Modena, just overlook it, because they haven't learned it very well yet. As far as the rest is concerned, I'm sure you're intelligent enough to pick it up without any trouble. you will learn, above all else, two things: how important good fortune and the right moment are in love, and how important patience accompanied by good advice it. Two young girls will demonstrate this with their wisdom, and by following their wisdom you will benefit as well, so you ladies should be grateful to us. These men, meanwhile, even if they don't enjoy our play, should still have plenty to thank us for, since for four hours, more or less, we'll be giving them the opportunity to contemplate your divine beauty. But I see two old men coming out on stage, so I will leave, unhappy to leave your beauty, even if I plan to return to see you again. Goodbye, all.

castItem.roleDesc: a young man, son of VIRGINIO
the daughter of the balia CLEMENZIA

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Virginio, if you want to make me happy, as you’ve promised, let’s arrange this holy matrimony quickly and get me out of this hopeless mess that has somehow overwhelmed me. And if something is holding you back, like not having enough money for clothes or furnishings for the house or if you’re unable to pay for the wedding right now, don’t worry – I know all too well that you lost everything in the terrible sack of Rome. Just tell me, and I’ll take care of everything. It wouldn’t be any problem for me to spend another ten scudi, especially if we could move this up a month to satisfy my eagerness. Thank God I have the money. And you know as well as I do that neither of us are spring chickens any longer, we’re pushing our prime a bit, and maybe… well, anyway, the older one gets the less time one has to lose. Don’t be surprised Virginio, if I press you, because I swear that since I’ve begun to dream of this, I haven’t had half a night’s sleep. Look at how early I was up this morning! Why, in order not to disturb you I heard the first mass at the cathedral before I came here. But if you have had a change of heart and have decided that your daughter’s too young for me, since I’m already well into my middle years and perhaps a bit beyond, tell me straight out. I’ll take care of it by turning my thoughts elsewhere. We’d both then avoid the problem, for, as you know, there’s no lack of others who would like to have me for a relative.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: None of these things are holding me back, Gherardo. If it was in my power to give you my daughter today, I would. But I lost virtually everything in the sack of Rome – including Fabrizio, my beloved son. Still, thank God, I have enough left that I hope I can pay to dress and marry my daughter without having to ask for help. Don’t worry that I want to break my promise, either. As long as the girl agrees, she’s yours, for as you know, a merchant needs to keep this promises.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Unfortunately, these days the promises of merchants are more upheld in words than in deeds. But you aren’t like the others, I’m sure. Still seeing myself put off day after day makes me worry that something is wrong. And knowing how forceful you are, I know that when you want to, you can make your daughter do what you want.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Let me explain. You know that I had to go to Bologna to close a deal that with Messer Buonaparte Chisilieri and the Cavalier da Casio. I was living alone in my country home and didn’t want to leave my daughter in the hands of the female servants there, so I sent her to the convent of San Crescenzio to stay with Sister Camilla, her aunt. She’s still there, because I only returned last night, as you know. Just know I sent a servant to have then send her home.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Are you sure she’s in the convent and not somewhere else?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Why shouldn’t she be there? Where else do you think she would be? What are you suggesting?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Well, I’ve been there several times on business of my own, and I’ve asked to see her but without success. And certain sisters have told me that she’s not there.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: That’s because those good sisters want her to become a nun in order to get what little remains of my wealth after I die. But their plan won’t work, for I’m not so old that I can’t still father a couple of sons when I take a wife.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Us, old? Why, I can tell you that I feel as strong and hard as I did when I was twenty-five, especially in the morning before I pee. Even if I have this white beard, between my legs I’m still as green as Boccaccio! And I defy any of these pansy-boys who prance around Modena trying to act tough with their hat feathers standing up stiff in the Guelph style, with their swords at their thigh, with their daggers hanging behind their ass, with their silk tassels – I defy them to outdo me at anything, except perhaps running.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You’ve a great heart, even if I don’t know how you’ll hold up.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You just ask Lelia how it held up after her first night with me!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: In God’s name, take it easy with her! She’s still young, and it’s not good to be too forceful in the beginning.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: How old is she?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: When we were prisoners of those swine, the Germans, during the sack of Rome, she was thirteen.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: That’s perfect for me. I don’t want a wife who’s too young or too old. I have the most beautiful clothes, the most beautiful jewels, the most beautiful necklaces, and the most beautiful accouterments for a woman of any man in Modena.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Excellent! I’m satisfied for her well-being and yours.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Press ahead, then!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: As far as the dowry’s concerned, we’ll stick to our agreement.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Do you think I would change my mind? Goodbye.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Good day to you.

p.seg: I wonder what to make of the fact that all my hens were so excited this morning. They made so much noise that it was as if they wanted to throw the house into confusion, or else make me rich with their eggs. Something strange is going to happen to me today; they never make such a commotion unless there's bad news or something goes wrong.
This woman must be talking with angels or with the blessed preacher of the Church of Saint Francis.
And another strange thing happened to me that I don't know how to interpret, even if my confessor told me that I shouldn't believe in such sings.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What are you doing, talking to yourself? They day of the Befana has already passed.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Oh! Good day, Virginio. In God's name, I came by to visit you for a little, but you'd already gone out. I'm very glad to see you back!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What were you mumbling to yourself just now? Were you planning to talk me out of some bushels of grain or bottles of oil or some lard, as usual?

p.seg: How easy it is to talk a magnanimous tightwad like him out of something! Is he perhaps putting away money for his children?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What were you saying, anyway?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I was saying that I didn't know what to make of the fact that a pretty kitty that disappeared fifteen days ago turned up this morning. And then she caught a mouse in my dark room, and while playing with it, she upset a flask of Trebbiano wine that the preacher of the Church of Saint Francis had given me for doing his wash.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: This is a sign that there'll be a wedding. But you wanted me to give you another flask of wine, right?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: See, I do know how to read signs! But where's Lelia, your nursling?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Oh, the poor child, it would've been better if she'd never been born!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You ask why? Isn't that Gherardo Foiani going around saying that she's his wife and that everything's arranged?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: He's telling the truth. Why not? Don't you think it's good that she'll be set up in an honorable house with a rich man, well furnished with all the goods one could ask for and without anyone else in the house, so she won't have to fight with a mother-in-law, a daughter-in-law, or a sister-in-law (usually they're at each other like cats and dogs)? And he'll treat her like a daughter.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: That's the problem: young girls want to be treated like wives, not daughters. They want me who sweep them off their feet, bite them, lay into them first from one side and then the other, not someone who treats them like a daughter.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You think all women are like you, and you know that I know you well enough! But she's not like that - even if Gherardo is more than ready to treat her as a wife.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: How? Why, he's already well over fifty!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What does that matter? I'm almost that old, and you know I'm still capable of giving you a good ride, right?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Oh my, there are few men your equal! But if I thought that you would really give her to him, I'd drown her first.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Clemenzia, I lost everything. Now I have to make do as best I can. If one day Fabrizio were to be found and I'd given everything away for her dowry, he'd die of hunger. And that I don't want. This way I can marry her to Gherardo with the proviso that if Fabrizio doesn't turn up within four years, she'll have a dowry of one thousand florins. If he does, she'll get only two hundred from me, and Gherardo will make up the rest.

p.seg: I know that if she did as I wish she would...

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What's she up to? How long has it been since you saw her?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: More than fifteen days. I wanted to visit her today.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I think those sisters want to make her a nun, and I'm afraid that as usual they've tried to put a bug in her ear. Go to the convent and tell them I want her to return home.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You know, I need you to lend me two carlini to buy some wood. I don't have a stick.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Devil, you never give up! Get going now, and I'll buy you some myself.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I want to go to mass first.

div2.head: Scene II
div2.stage: LELIA (dressed as a boy) and CLEMENZIA

p.seg: Leaving the house alone at this hour requires real courage when one considers the evil ways of the rowdy young men of Modena! Oh, it would serve me right of one of those young rogues forced me into one of these houses to see for himself whether I was a boy or a girl! That would teach me to be out so early! But I'm here because I love that fickle and cruel Flamminio. Oh, how unlucky I am! I love someone who hates me, who is always cursing me. I serve someone who doesn't even recognize me. And to make matters worse, I help him in his pursuit of another woman - who would believe it! - without any other hope than so satisfy my desire to see him one day at a time. And actually up to this point everything has gone pretty well.But what I am I to do now? What strategy can I use? My father has returned, Flamminio has come to live in the city, and I can't stay here without being recognized. But if that should happen, I'd be dishonored forever and become a scandal in the whole city. So I'm out at this hour to ask the advice of my balia, whom I saw come this way form the window. Together we can decide on the best strategy. But first I want to see if she recognizes me in this get-up!

My goodness, Flamminio must have returned to Modena, for I see his door is open. Oh, if Lelia knew, she would be eager to return home! But who is this young showoff cutting back and forth in front of me in the street this morning?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: God give you a good day, Lady Sponger.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Save your "good days" for someone you ought to have said good night to.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Even if I did say good night to someone else, I want to say good day to you, if you'll let me.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Don't give me a hard time, or I'll tell you what you'll make me do to you this morning?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Are you waiting for the preacher of the Church of Saint Francis, perhaps, or are you going to Fra Cipollone?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Shoo! Go to hell! What's it to you where I'm going or who I'm going to see? Keep your nose out of my business! What preacher? What Fra Cipollone?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh, don't get all upset, Lady-Full-of-Threats-but-without-Deeds!

p.seg: I'm certain I know this kid, but I don't know form where, even though it seems like I've seen his face a thousand times.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Come on! Are you pretending you don't recognize me?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: If you keep hiding behind that cape, neither I nor anyone else will recognize you.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Come this way a little.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Over here. [Pulling back her cape] Now do you recognize me?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Is that you, Lelia? Oh, my life is ruined! What a disaster! Yes, it's you! Good heavens! What does this mean, my dear child?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Be quiet. You’re acting like a madwoman. If you keep shouting, I'll leave.

p.seg: Is she the least but ashamed?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Yes, I'm of the world. How many women have you seen from outside the world? As far as I'm concerned, I don't remember ever being outside the world.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: But have you lost, then, the name of virgin?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: The name, no - not as far as I know, especially here in Modena. For the rest, you'll have to ask the Spaniards who held me prisoner in Rome.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Is this the honor you owe to your father, your house, yourself, and you me who nursed you? Why, I could cut your throat with my own hands! Come along, now, I don't want you to be seen out here in these clothes.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh, please calm down!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Aren't you ashamed to be seen like this?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Am I perhaps the first woman who ever dressed like this? I've seen hundreds in Rome. And in Modena there are plenty of women who go about their business every night dressed like this.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: They're wicked women!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh well, among so many wicked women isn't there room for one good much?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I want to know way you’re running arround like this and why you left the convent. Oh, if your father knew, he’d have your head, poor child!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: That would solve my problems. Do you think I value mi life all that much?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Why are you running around like this? Tell me.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I'll explain, if you'll listen. And then you'll understand my misfortune and why I left the convent dressed like this and what I need you to do for me. But come this way a bit so that if anyone passes by they won't recognize me talking with you.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You're driving me crazy. Tell me quickly, or I'm going to die of desperation! Oh my!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: You know that after the horrible sack of Rome, my father, having lost everything, including my brother Fabrizio, in order not to live alone took me away from the Lady Marchesana in whose service he had left me earlier. Our poverty forced us to return to our home here in Modena to escape our evil fortune and live as well as we could with what little we had. And you know that my father, because he had been a close friend of Count Guido Rangone, was not well received here by some.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Why are you telling me what I already know better than you do? And I know that this was the reason that you both went to stay on your farm at Fontanile and I went with you.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Exactly. You remember also how difficult and hard my life was then. My thoughts were not only far from love but far from virtually everything human. For I was afraid that having been in the hands of Spanish soldiers, everyone would be pointing at me. I was certain that no matter times you scolded me and urged me to be happier?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: If, as you say, I know this already, why are you telling me again? But go on.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Well, if I hadn't repeated it, you wouldn't be able to understand the rest. It so happened that at that time, because Flamminio Carandini was one of our faction, he became a close friend of my father. Day after day he came to our house and sometimes very secretly he would look at me, sigh, and lower his eyes. You were the one who pointed it out to me. I began to enjoy his manners and conversation and his way of carrying himself much more than I did at first. But I wasn't thinking of love. Still, visiting our house, he made me aware of how much he was taken with me, first with one thing and then with many sings of love, sighs, longing gazes, and glances, so that although I'd never been in love before, felling that he was worthy of love I began to turn my thoughts towards him, and eventually I fell for him so completely that to see him was my only desire.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I knew all his already, also.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: And you will remember that when all the soldiers finally left Rome, my father wanted to go back partly to see if any of our possessions were still there, but mainly to see if he could learn anything about my brother. And because he didn't want to leave me alone, he sent me to Mirandola to live with my aunt Giovanna until he came back. How unhappy I was to be separated from my Flamminio, you know well, for many times you dried my tears! I remained at Mirandola for a year. Then when my father came back, as you know, we returned to Modena, and I was more than ever in love with Flamminio. Since he was my first love, I was very happy, assuming that he would love me as he did before.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Silly little girl! How many men of Modena do you know who'd be able to love a woman a whole year rather than deceiving first one for a while and then another?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: When I found him, in fact, I might just as well have never existed as far as he was concerned. And what was worse, he was committed heart and soul to winning the love of Isabella, the daughter of Gherardo Foiani, who not only is very beautiful but also is his only heir, if that old madman doesn't decide to marry and have other children.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Gherardo believes that his marriage with you is all arranged, and he's going around saying that your father has given his word. But all this still doesn't explain why you're running around dressed like a man or why you've left the convent.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Let me finish, and you'll understand. But as far as Gherardo is concerned, I can tell you that he'll never have me. After my father returned from Rome, he had to go to Bologna on business. And because I didn't want to return to Mirandola, he put me in the convent of San Crescenzio with our relative, Sister Amabile, while he was away, which supposed to be for a shot time only.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I knew all this.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Living there, I found that the reverend mothers didn't talk about anything except love. So it seemed to me that I could reveal my love as well to Sister Amabile de'Cortesi. Taking pity on me, she worked day and night to get Flamminio to come to the convent to talk with her and the other nuns so that hidden behind a curtain, I could comfort my eyes and ears looking at him, I heard him lamenting the death of a young boy in his service and singing his praises. And he said that if he could find another boy like that, he would trust him with everything he owned and be the happiest person in the world.

p.seg: Woe is me! I'm afraid that this "boy" business is going to make my life very unhappy.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I immediately decided that I wanted to see if I could become that lucky boy. So as soon as he left, I broached the subject with Sister Amabile. Since Flamminio was not living in Modena, I wanted to see if I could become his servant and get away with it.

p.seg: Didn't I say that this "boy" - ... I'm ruined!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: She agreed with me and showed me how I should act, giving me some clothes that she has recently made for herself so that she could leave the convent every now and then on her own business dressed as a man like the other sisters. So one morning earl, I left the convent in these clothes, and being outside of Modena, I was quite confident and things went very smoothly. I went to the villa where Flamminio was living, which as you know is not far from the convent, and I waited there until he came out. In this I must thank Fortune, for the minute Flamminio saw me he asked me very courteously where I was from and if I has anything to ask him.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Didn't you die of shame on the spot?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Actually, with the help of Love, I answered him earnestly that I was a Roman seeking my fortune because of my poverty. He looked me up and down from head to toe several times so closely that I was afraid he would recognize me. Then he said that if I was agreeable he would gladly take me on and that he would treat me well and as a gentleman. And although I felt a bit embarrassed, I accepted.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Listening to you, I wish I'd never been born! What good did you see in such craziness?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: What good? Does it seem to you a small thing for a woman in love to be able to see her lord all the time, to speak with him, touch him, hear his secrets, meet his friends and discuss things with him, and be sure that if she's not enjoying him, at least no one else is?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: These are the way of a foolish child. They don't accomplish anything beyond adding wood to the fire, unless you think they make the man you love happier. But how do you serve him?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: At the table, in the bedroom. And I know that he's been so pleased with me in these fifteen days that if I'd been wearing my regular dress, I would feel truly blessed!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Wait just a minute - where do you sleep?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: In a small room off his bedroom, alone.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What would happen if one night, moved by an evil lust, he should call you to sleep with him?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: There's no sense worrying about problems before they occur. If it happens, I'll think it over and decide.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What will people say when they learn about this, you naughty little girl?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Who's going to say anything, if you don't tell? Now, this is what I want you to do, because I've learned that my father returned last night, and I imagine he'll send for me: see to it that for four or five days he doesn't. Or tell him that I've gone with Sister Amabile to Roverino and that I'll return in four or five days.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I'll tell you. Flamminio, as I told you earlier, is in love with Isabella Foiani, and often, very often, he sends me to her with letters and messages. She, however, has fallen madly in love with me thinking that I'm a man and gives me the sweetest caresses ever. Meanwhile, I'm pretending that I don't want to be her lover unless she makes Flamminio forget about her. I've already brought matters to a head, and I'm hoping that in the next three or four days everything will come together and he'll leave her.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I'm afraid that your father has already asked me to get you. So I want you to come to my house now so that I can send for your clothes. You shouldn't be seen like this. And if you don't do as I say, I'll tell your father everything.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: If you do, you'll be responsible for me going where neither of you will ever see me again. Do as I ask, please! [Seeing GHERARDO coming out his house] But I can't tell you the whole story now. I hear Flamminio calling me. [Calling as if to FLAMMINIO] My lord! [To CLEMENZIA] Wait for me an hour from now at your house; I'll meet you there. And you should know that if you want to find me, you should ask for Fabio degli Alberini, which is the name I've taken. Don't forget. [Calling as if to FLAMMINIO] I'm coming, sir! [To CLEMENZIA] Goodbye.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: My goodness, she saw Gherardo, who's headed this way, and she's disappeared. What am I to do now? I can't tell her father, and I can't let her stay here like this. I'll keep quiet until we speak again.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: If Virginio keeps his promise, I'm going to be giving myself the best time of any man in Modena. What do you think, Spela? Wouldn't that be something?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: I think it would be much better if you gave something to your nephews, who need it, or to me, since I've served you so long that I've worn the soles off my shoes. I'm afraid that this wife will send you over the edge or give you a set of- ... actually, I'm sure of it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You'll see that she'll be well paid by me.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: I believe you. While other men would satisfy her with good hard coin, you'll pay her with tiny little hapfpennies.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [As CLEMENZIA approaches] Here's her balia. Be quiet, while I cleverly ask her know Lelia is.

p.seg: What a handsome lily fresh from the garden that Gherardo is to want a wife so young! Who would ever think it was a good idea to hand that poor child over to this wheezing old geezer? By the holy cross, I'd suffocate her before I'd let her be given to that run-down, moldy, drooling, rancid snotnose. I want to work him over a bit. I'll go over to him.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: And may God give you a hundred thousand and more ducats.

p.seg: Those would be better given to me.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, Spela, how happy I'd be if I were Clemenzia!

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Because you would've gotten to try a bunch of husbands rather than just the one wife you've had? Or are you trying to say something else?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: And according to you, just how many husbands have I tried, Spela? May God have the flies skin you alive! Are you jealous that you weren't one of them?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Sure, by God! But I don't know if I could have handled all the pleasure!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Shut up, you idiot. I wasn't saying that at all.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: What were you saying, then?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I meant that if I were she, I would so often have hugged, kissed, and held to my breast my sweet Lelia, made of sugar, of gold, of milk, of roses, and so much else that I'm at a loss for words.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Oh, oh, my master, let's go indoors! Get going! Hurry up!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: You have a fever, and staying out here in the air will make it worse.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I have only the pain in the butt that I hope God will give you. What fever? I feel perfectly fine.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: I'm sure that you have a fever, and I'm certain that it's a big one.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I know that I feel fine.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Does your head hurt?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Let me take your pulse. Does your stomach hurt, or do you feel some sort of vapor rising to you brain?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You've lost your mind! DO you want to make me into a Calandrino, perhaps? I tell you, I don't have any problem other than missing my Lelia, so delicate, so sweet.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: I'm certain that you have a fever and that you're very sick.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: How can you tell?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: How? Can’t you see that you're out of your mind, raving, frenzied, and that you don't know what you're saying?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: It's love that makes me act like that, right, Clemenzia? Omnia vincit amor!

p.seg: Right! What a beautiful! Neapolitan saying! Facetis manum, everybody: it's never been said before.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: That sweet cruel one, you little daughter, sweet traitor...

p.seg: This isn't a fever, this is a terminal idiocy. Oh my! Woe is me! What can I do?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, Clemenzia, I want to hug and kiss you a thousand times!

p.seg: I'm afraid we need ropes to tie the madman down.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Watch out! I've no desire to be kissed by and old man.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Do I seem to you that old?

p.seg: What do you think? At least my master's eyes haven't fallen out of his mouth yet - oops, I mean his teeth.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Well, now that I take a better look at you, I can say that you aren't as old as you seem.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Tell Lelia that. And listen, if you put in a good word for me with her, I'll give you a veil.

p.seg: Wow, the big spender! And what will you give me?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: If you were as much in the graces of the duke of Ferran as you are in the graces of Lelia, how lucky you would be! Yes, of course! But who are you kidding? If you really loved her, you wouldn't be doing this to her or trying to ruin her life.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What do you mean, ruin her life? I'm trying to give her a good life, not ruin it.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Why have you kept her waiting a whole year with your negotiations over whether or not you would marry her?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What? Does Lelia think that was my fault, then? Why, if you should find that I didn't ask her father every day, that this hasn't been my greatest desire, that I didn't wish to marry her immediately, may you see me laid out in my coffin sooner rather than later.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: With God's grace, let's hope that's the case! I'll tell her everything. But do you realize that she'd prefer to see you dressed differently? Now you look like an old goat.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What do you mean, old goat? What have I done?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Nothing, but you're always out all wrapped up in animal skins of one kind or another.

p.seg: To win her love, then, he'd be better off if he has himself skinned alive or at least went naked through the streets. Can you believe it?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I have the finest clothes of any man in Modena. Still, I'm grateful for your advice, and she'll soon find that I have a different look. But where will I be able to see her when she returns from the convent?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: At the Bazzovara gate. I'm going to get her right now.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Why don't you let me come with you? We could talk as we walk.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: No, no. What would people say?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'm dying. Oh, love!

p.seg: I'm bursting with laughter. Oh, heaven above!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, how blessed you are!

p.seg: Oh, you're crazier by far!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, Clemenzia, so lucky!

p.seg: Oh, blockhead, so ducky!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, milk of kindliness!

p.seg: Oh, brains of emptiness!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, Clemenzia, so joyful and dear!

p.seg: Oh, you, so full in the rear!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Go on now, Clemenzia! Goodbye. [CLEMENZIA leaves] Come along now, Spela, I want to refashion myself. I've decided to dress myself more stylishly to please my wife.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: This is going to end badly.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Because you're already beginning to do things her way. She's going to wear the pants in the family.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Go to the shop of Marco, the perfume maker, and buy me a jar of musk. I'm ready to lead the live of a lover.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Where's the moner?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Here, take this bolognino. And be quick about it. I'm going home.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: [Alone] If anyone wished to wrap up all the foolishness in the world in one package, they could wrap up my master and the job would be done. And now that he has embarked on this mad passion of love, it's even more true. He shaves, he combs his fair, he paces back and forth before her house, he goes out at night to parties armed with dagger, he goes about all day caterwauling with that raspy, coarse voice of his and a lute even more out of tune than his singing. And he has even given himself to writing efistulas (may he come down with one) - snotnets, rhyndes, stramboats, mad-gals, and a thousand other things that belong in comedies. It's enough to make the asses of this world die laughing, never mind the dogs! Now he wants to start putting on musk. In God's name, it's enough to make even one's balls go crazy. But here's Scatizza, who ought to be coming back from the convent.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: [Muttering to himself] Why, these fathers who have their daughters made nuns must be just like the great men of the time of Bartolomeo Coglioni. Can they really believe that their daughters spend all their time on their knees before crucifix praying to God that he reward them for putting them in the convent? It's true that they pray to God, and the devil as well, but asking rather that they break the necks of those who've has then locked up in there.

p.seg: I want to hear this story.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: [Still muttering to himself] As soon as I knocked at the supposedly locked door into the inner cloisters, the room filled with nuns, all young and as beautiful as angels. I started to ask for Lelia. On one side some laughed, on the other side some giggled, and then they all began to play around with me as if I were a sweet hard candy.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: God bless you, Scatizza! Where are you coming from? Sure, you have the sweetest candy. Let me try some.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: A pox on you and that madman, you master!

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Leave alone, and keep the pox for yourself. Bbut where are you coming from?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: From the nuns of San Crescenzio.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: All right, but what about Lelia? Has she returned home?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: May the gallows return for you! Can God allow that imbecile, you master, to think that he's going to have her?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Why not? Doesn't she want him?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: I really doubt it. Does she strike you as being meat for his teeth?

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: She's right not to want him. But what did she say?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: She didn't say a thing. What could she say, considering that I didn't get to see her? When I go there and asked for her, those hungry nuns wanted to make a snack of me.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: They wanted more than a snack! More like the meat course. You clearly don't know them.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: I know them better than you, may the pox take them! You should have been there. The first one wanted to know if I was lovesick, then another if I would marry her. Yet another said that Lelia was all wet in the bath and drying herself off, and one said that she was all tied up at the moment in the sleeping quarters. One asked me, "Did you father have any male children?" Oh! I was about to say to her, "I have a large co- ... cock-a-doodle-do," but finally I realized that they were just kidding around and that they didn't want to me to talk with Lelia.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: You really weren't very clever. You should've marched right in and told them you wanted to look around for her yourself.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Are you crazy? Go rught in there by myself? Come on, man, come on. Do you want to see me ruined? Oh, there isn't a stallion in the Maremma who could stand up to them alone! Nuns? A pox on hem! But I can't hang around here any longer, I have to get back to my master.

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: And I have to buy some musk, for my own crazy one.

div2.head: SCENE I
div2.stage: LELIA (dressed as a boy) and FLAMMINIO

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: It's very disheartening that after all this time you still haven't been able to win a kind word for me form that cruel and ungrateful Isabella. Still, to see you always welcomed so warmly and listened to so willingly makes me think that she doesn't hate me. And as far as I know, I've never done anything to displease her. You'd now form what she said if she was upset with me about anything. But please tell me again, Fabio, what she said to you last night when you took her my letter.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I've already told you twenty times.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Well, tell me again. What's it to you?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: What's it to me? It makes me sad to see you so downcast; it makes me suffer as much as you. Since I'm your servant, I don't want to give you anything by pleasure, and I worry that her replies will make you unhappy with me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Don't worry, my dear Fabio. I love you like a brother, and I know that you love me, so you can be sure I'll never let you down, as you'll see with time. Say your prayers and don't worry about anything else. But what did she say?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: As I told you already:that the greatest pleasure you could give her in the whole world would be to leave her alone and stop thinking about her because she's fallen in love with someone else; and that she can't stand the sight of you anymore and you're wasting your time courting her, because when all is said and done, you're going to find yourself empty-handed.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Did it seem to you that she really meant it, or is she upset with me about something? There was a time when every now and then she seemed to like me, and I really can't believe that she dislikes me that much, for she accepts my letters and messages. I'm prepared to court her until the day I die. At least I want to see what the future has to offer. What do you think, Fabio? Don't you agree?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I don't, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Because if I were in your shoes, I'd want her to be happy with my courtship. What woman would pass up a man like you, noble, accomplished, gentle-mannered, and handsome? Take my advice, Master:drop her and find someone else who loves you. You'll have no trouble finding another and, yes, perhaps one just as beautiful. Tell me, haven't you ever loved another who appreciated your attentions here in Modena?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Of course. There was one among the others called Lelia - in fact, many times I have been tempted to say that you remind me of her. She's reputed to be the most beautiful, wise, and well-mannered young woman in these parts - I should point her out to you someday. She would be very pleased if I showed her a bit of favor. She's rich and has been at court. And she was my love for about a year, showing me much favor, until she went off to Mirandola. Then my evil fortune make me fall in love with this woman who's been as cruel to me as the other was gentle.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Master, turn about is fair play. You have ignored someone who loves you; it's only fair that now you are being ignored.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What are you trying to say?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: If that poor young woman was your first love and she continues to love you more than ever, why have you abandoned her to run after another? I'm not sure that God can ever forgive such a sin. Heavens, my lord Flamminio! You're clearly very much in the wrong.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You're still a boy, Fabio, and you don't understand the power of love. Look, I'm forced to love and adore this new woman, and I can't think about anyone else. I don't know how to, and I'm not cpaable of it. So go talk to her again and see if you can wheedle out of her why she's so upset with me that she doesn't want to see me.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: You're wasting your time.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I'm willing to waste this time.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: You're not going to accomplish anything.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: That's life!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Give up on her, I say.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I can't. Go on, do as I ask.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I'm going, but ...

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Come back immediately with her reply. I'll walk on the cathedral.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: As soon as the moment is right, I'll give it my best shot.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Fabio, if you can do it, I'll be very pleased with you!

p.seg: We split up just in time, because here comes Pasquella looking for me.

div2.head: SCENE II
div2.stage: PASQUELLA and LELIA (dressed as a boy)

p.seg: I don't believe there's a greater pain or hassle in the whole world for someone like me than to serve a young girl in love. And that's even more true when that girl doesn't have to fear her mother, sister, or other person, like my mistress. Recently she's fallen so madly in love and become so lathered up that she can't find any peace, day or night. She's always scratching between her legs, stroking her thighs, or running up onto the porch or over to the window or running down the stairs or up the stairs. She just can't seem to stop; it's as if she had quicksilver in her feet. For God's sake, oh, yes, I too was young once and in love as well, and I did some little things that I shouldn't have done, but I also calmed down from time to time.It would be better, however, if only she'd decided to fall in love with someone of worth, someone mature, a man who would know how to take care of his business and scratch her itch. But she's all caught up with a fancy boy who looks like he would have trouble buttoning up his pants without help if they were unbuttoned. And all day long she sends me to finds this lover-boy, as if I didn't have any work to do around the house. Can his master really think that he's acting on his behalf? But this is certainly him coming along now. What luck!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: And may God give you a thousand scudi, my dear Pasquella. What's your pretty mistress up to? What does she want form me?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What do you think she's going? She's crying, she's all upset, she a mess because you haven't visited her yet this morning.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: My goodness, what does she want? Does she want me to het there before the sun comes up?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I imagine she'd like to have you stay the whole night, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Well, I have other things to do. I have to serve my master. Do you understand, Pasquella?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Well, I'm sure your master would feel that you were serving him in coming here, right? But wait, are you perhaps sleeping with him?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I wish to God he liked me that much! If that were the case I wouldn't be in the mess I'm in.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh my! But wouldn't you rather sleep with Isabella?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Not me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What? You're not serious!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I wish I weren't!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Hmmm. Well, let's change the subject. My mistress told me to ask you to come visit her right away because her father isn't at home and she needs to speak with you about something important.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Tell her that she's just wasting her time if she doesn't get rid of Flamminio first. She knows that I'd be ruined otherwise.

sp.speaker: PASQUELA:
sp.p: Come tell her yourself.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I said I had other things to do. Didn't you hear me?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What do you have to do that's so important? Run over to see her, and you can hurry right back.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh, you're a pain in the neck. Get lost.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Won't you come?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I said no. Can't you undestand?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: In good faith and in all honesty I'll tell you, Fabio, you're too arrogant. Remember that you're just a young dandy, and you don't really understand how lucky you are. But this fascination with you isn't going to last forever, you know. You're going to grow a beard, you cheeks aren't going to remain so fresh, your lips so red. You won't always be so sought after by everyone - no, sir. Then you'll realize what a fool you've been, and you'll regret what you missed when it's too late. Tell me, how many men do you think there are in this city who'd be delighted if Isabella even smile at them? And do you think you can just laugh at such a sweet dish!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Well, why doesn't she smile at one of them, then, and leave me alone? I'm not interested.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: My God! It's obvious that these youngsters today don't have enough good sense to get by.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Come on, Pasquella! Don't keep preaching at me, you'll only make it worse.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Stuck up, stuck up, you're going to miss being so stuck up when you grown up! Come on, my dear, sweet Fabio, my soul! COme, for goodness sake, quickly. If you don't, she'll just send me out again to find you because she won't believe I've talked with you.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Fine. Relax! I'll come, Pasquella. I was just kidding.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: When, my sweet?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Soon.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: How soon?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Soon enough. Now get lost.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I'll be waiting for you at the door, all right?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: And, uh, you know that if you don't show up, I'll be mad.

p.seg: For the life of me, if this isn't the lucky old bag who serves the most beautiful young thing in this city! What I wouldn't give to have two words alone with her! By the vow of virginity of all the clerics of Rome, I swear I'd make her howl like a cat in heat! But for now, let me see if I can sweet-talk this old bag into helping me with her mistress.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh! Good day, Giglio. I'm coming from mass. Where are you going?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Seeking my fortune. I'm looking for a woman who would be give me some kindness.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, sure! That's exactly what you Spaniards need! Why, there's not a one of you who doesn't have a dozen women hanging around.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: It's true that I have two myself, but I can't visit them anymore without danger.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What? Are they gentlewomen if the Easylay family, perhaps?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Yes, by my word, exactly. But now I want a mother who'll wash my shirts sometimes and mend by socks and jacket and keep me like a son. And I'll help her with good service.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Keep looking, keep on looking; no doubt you'll find plenty. A man like you who already has his gentlewomen will have no trouble finding servants.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I've already found someone, with your permission.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: You yourself.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Really! But I'm too old for you.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Old? I swear by the Virgin Mary of Monserrat that you seem to me a sweet thing of fifteen or twenty. Old? Don't ever say such a thing again, because I can't bear to hear it. If you decide to be kind to me, you'll see soon enough whether I treat you like a young woman or an old me!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: No, no, Spanish Rooster, get lost! I don't want to get involved with Spaniards. You're like horse flies, either you bite or you harass, and you're like coal, either you burn or you blacken. We've has plenty of experience with you by now, unfortunately for us! We know you well, thank God. And there's clearly nothing to be gained from becoming involved with you.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Gain? I swear to God that you will gain more from me than from the most important gentleman of this city! And although I may appear to you now to be down on my luck, I can tell you that I come from one of the most noble families in all Spain.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: It's a miracle that you didn't claim to be a lord or a knight! All the Spaniards who come here make themselves lords. And then take a look at how they behave!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Pasquella, accept my friendship. It will bring you great benefit!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What will you do for me? Make me a lady, maybe?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I'm not asking you to be anything except my mother. And I want to be your son and sometimes also your husband, if that would please you.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Laughing] Oh, leave me alone!

p.seg: Ah, she's laughing. Let's see if this puts her in the carnival spirit.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What did you say?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: That I want to give you a rosary to say during carnival.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: And where is it?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Here it is.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, it's beautiful! Why don't you give it to me?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: If you'll be my mother, I'll give it to you.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I'll be whatever you want, if you give it to me.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: When can we talk alone together for an hour?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Whenever you wish.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, I don't know where.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Isn't there someplace in the house where you can keep me tonight?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Yes, there is. But what if my master should find out?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: What? Don't worry, he won't find out anything!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Look, I'll see if it's possible tonight. Come by the house, and I'll tell you if you can come in or not. Now give me that rosary. Oh, it is beautiful!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Good. I'll be here to find out at nightfall.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Right, yes! But give me the rosary.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I'll bring it with me when I return. I want to have it perfumed a little for you first.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: There's no need for that. Give it to me as it is; I don't want it more perfumed.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Look, this piece is broken. I'll have it replaced with a bit of gold, then I'll give it to you this evening. There's no rush, it will be yours.

p.seg: It will be mine when I have it. One can't rely very much on the word of you Spaniards, I'm afraid. I'm not the only one who says that you're like the tax collector:whatever happens, you never give, only take.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: What are you saying, my mother?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I have to go inside, my mistress is waiting for me.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Wait just a little longer. What's the rush? What do you have to do for your mistress?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, you wouldn't believe it. May the devil take me if these young girls nowadays don't fall in love before they're dry behind the ears and if they aren't ready to use the pestle and mortar before the needle and thread.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: What are you trying to say?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Dying to say? Why, I'm just trying to say that she really would like to start grinding away!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: But it's no possible, she's still too young. Please tell me who she's in love with.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I wish it weren't true, or at least that she was in love with someone worthy of her.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Tell me, on your life, who is he?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I don't want to say. Look, you must keep this a secret. Do you know that boy who serves Flamminio de'Cardini?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Who? That kid that goes around all dressed in white?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Yes, him.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Good God! It is possible? How could she want to be served by him? He's more fit for being screwed than for screwing.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You got that right.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: And that boy, does he love the girl?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Well, more or less.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Doesn't her father know about this?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I don't think so. Actually, he has twice discovered him in the house and given him a thousand little caresses, taking his hand and chucking him under the chin as if he were his son. And he says that he thinks he resembles a daughter of Virginio Bellenzini.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Ah, damn that boy! Ah, that old pig, that lecher! Yes, yes, I know what he's after.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Ugh! You've kept me too long. I must go.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Remember that I'll come tonight. Don't forget your promise!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: And you, don't forget that rosary!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You haven't gone to look for Fabio, and he hasn't returned. I don't know what to make of his delay.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I was going, and then you called me back. Is that my fault?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Well, go now, and if he's at Isabella's, wait for him outside and when he comes out send him here immediately.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Well, how can I tell if he's there or not? Do you want me to ask her if he's there?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What an ass! Do you think that would be a good idea? It's clear that I don't have anyone to serve me who's worth a fig besides Fabio. God help me reward him as he deserves! And you, what are you muttering about? Do you have something to say, you knave? Isn't it true?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: What do you do want to me to say? I say yes, of course. Fabio is good. Fabio is handsome. Fabio serves well. Fabio with you, Fabio with your girl. Fabio is everything, Fabio does everything. But ...

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: But what?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: He may not be entirely the right stuff.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What are you suggesting with this "stuff" thing?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: That you can't always trust him. Look, he's a foreigner, and one day he could carry off your stuff.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I wish I had a much faith in you others as I have in him! [SCATIZZA enters] Here's Scatizza, ask him if he's seen Fabio. I'll be at the Porrini bank.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Hello, Scatizza. Have you seen Fabio?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Who? Your boy with the right stuff? That little bastard! You can have him.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Where are you headed?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: To find my old boss.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: He left just a moment ago.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Where did he go?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: They way. Come on, and we'll catch up with him. Hurry up! I have a funny story to tell you about what happened to me with my Caterina - the best story ever!

sp.speaker: SPELA:
sp.p: Could there be a worse thing in the world than to serve a master who's crazy? Gherardo sent me to buy musk. When I told the apothecary that I had only one bolognino, he insisted that Gherardo wouldn't know what to do with musk. So I began to explain Gherardo's mad love so that he would believe me, and he, along with several other young fellows who were there, almost died laughing. He even wanted me to take him a jar of asafetida, so I left with laughter ringing in my ears. Now if my master wants that musk, he'll have to give me more money.

div2.head: SCENE VI
div2.stage: CRIVELLO, SCATIZZA, LELIA (dressed as a boy), and ISABELLA

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: So that's it. And if you want to come, I'll do everything to find a girl for you too.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: See what you can do, and I promise you that if you find me a cute serving girl, we'll have a great time together. I have the keys to the granary, to the wine cellar, to the pantry, to the wood, and if you get me an easy lay, I'll make us rich in any other way.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Good, I'll ask Bita to find you some easy piece so that all four of us can have a good time together this carnival.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Yeah! But it's already the last day of carnival.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: We'll have us a good time during Lent, then, while our masters are praying and only dreaming of women. But wait a second, Gherardo's door is opening. Let's hide over here for a bit.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Oh, let's say out of good manners.

div2.stage: [They move off as LELIA and ISABELLA appear in the doorway]

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: All right, Isabella! But don't forget what you promised.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: And don't forget to come to see me. Listen to me a second.

p.seg: If I were in the place of that pansy, I know my master wouldn't be able to forgive me.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: You'd have the chick for yourself, eh?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: What do you think?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Now what else do you want?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Listen a little.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: I'm listening.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Do you see anyone out in the street?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Not a living soul.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: What the devil is she up to?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: No good; they're too close.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Let's wait and see.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Listen, just a word.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: They're very close together.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: That's it! That's it!

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: You know, I would like...

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: What would you like?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: I would like... come a little closer.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Get closer yet, you animal!

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: See if there's anyone out there.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Didn't I tell you there's no one?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Oh, I'd like you to come back after dinner when my father will me away.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: All right. But when my master passes by, be sure to shut the window in his face and run off.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: If I don't, you needn't love me anymore.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Where the devil does she have her hands?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Oh, my poor master! But that's it, of course, I've got it now!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Goodbye.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Wait a second. Do you really want to leave?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Go ahead, kiss her. May you get the pox!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: She's afraid to be seen.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Go on, now. Go back in the house.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: I want one favor form you.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Come this way a little more into de doorway.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: The deed is all but done!

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: [As LELIA pulls away] Oh, you're so difficult!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: We'll be seen.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Oh my! Oh my! Oh damn! Why not me?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Didn't tell you he'd kiss her?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I'll tell you right out, I would rather have seen that kiss than earn a hundred scudi.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: I saw it, but I would rather have had it!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: My God! What will my master do when he hears about this?

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: In the devil's name, who would want to tell him?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Forgive me. You're so good looking and my love for you is so strong that I couldn't resist doing what you may well consider immodest for a young girl. But God knows, I couldn't stop myself.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: You don't need to ask me for forgiveness, madam, for I know only too well my own feelings and the things that I've done because I loved too much.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: What things?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh, what things? ... Deceiving my master, that's hardly good.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Oh, to hell with him!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: That's what faith in such trash will get you! It serves him right. No wonder the little fraud has been encouraging my master to forget this love!

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Everyone looks after good old number one. And in the end, all women are the same.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: It's late, and I must find my master. Goodbye.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: Wait a second.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Wow! And now it's two! May he dry up and go limp!

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: My God, I've got a leg so hard it seems ready to explode!

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Close the door, now. Goodbye.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA:
sp.p: I'm totally yours.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: And I'm yours. [ISABELLA goes in, and LELIA walks slowly away soliloquizing, unheard by CRIVELLO and SCATIZZA] On the one hand I'm having the best time ever playing with woman who believes I'm a man. On the other, I want to get out of this muddle and am not sure how. It's clear that she's already at the kissing stage, and who knows what will happen the next time we're together? And if she discovers my disguise, I'll lose everything. I need to find Clemenzia and see what she suggests. [Looking offstage] But here comes Flamminio.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Scatizza, my master told me that he would meet me at the Porrini bank. I want to give him the good news. But if he doesn't believe me, you must support me.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: You can count on me. Still, if it were up to me, I'd keep quiet and hold this knife to Fabio throat so he'd be forced to do whatever you wish.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: No, I want to get him. He has ruined me.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: It's up to you.

div2.stage: [He and CRIVELLO leave in the opposite direction from where FLAMMINIO enters; inside the house, ISABELLA slams the shutters closed as FLAMMINIO passes by the window]

div2.head: SCENE VII
div2.stage: FLAMMINIO and LELIA (dressed as a boy)

p.seg: Can I be so madly in love and think so little of myself that I want to love and serve a woman who despises me, who tortures me, who doesn't give a damn about me, who doesn't even want to give me the pleasure of a glance? Am I so worthless, so wile that I don't know how to end this shame and torture? But here's Fabio.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Why did it take you so long to return? Are you becoming gallows-bait?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: It took longer because I wanted to talk with Isabella.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Why didn't you talk with her?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: She didn't even want to listen to me. If you want my advice, I'd suggest you find another game and take care of yourself, because from everything I've seen to this point, you're wasting your time. She seems absolutely determined never to do anything that would please you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Well, even if God said it, He would be wrong. Yet do you know that just now, when I was walking by her house, the minute she saw me she ran from the window with such distaste and anger - almost as if she had seen something horrible or frightening?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Forget her, I say. It is possible that in his entire city there isn't some other woman who merits your love as much as she does? Haven't you ever been attracted to another woman?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I wish it weren't true! But I'm afraid that that might be the root of all my problems, because I loved with all my heart that Lelia, daughter of Virginio Bellenzini, whom I told you about. And I'm afraid that Isabella may think I'm still in love with her, and that's why she doesn't want to see me. But I'll convince her that I don't love Lelia anymore - in fact, that I hate her and can't stand even to hear her name. And I'll promise her absolutely never to ho near Lelia again. I want you to tell her this clearly.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh dear!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What's wrong? You seem about to faint. How do you feel?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh dear!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Where does it hurt?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: Oh dear! My heart.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How long have you had this? Lean on me a moment. Does your body ache?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: No, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Is your stomach upset?

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: It's my heart that hurts.

p.seg: Life is so strange! I wouldn't trade this Fabio for all my wealth, for I don't believe there's anyone more able or willing to serve me in all the world or better mannered than this young man. Moreover, he shows me so much love that if he were a woman, I would think that he's ill because he loves me.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: [Walking off] O poor wretch! Now you have heard with your own ears from the mouth of this ungrateful Flamminio just how much he loves you! Poor, sad Lelia! Why waste any more time serving this cruel man? Your patience, your prayers, your favors have done no good. Now event your deceptions have failed. Poor me! Rejected! Cast aside! Fled! Hated! What am I doing serving the man who rejects me? Why am I staying with the man who cast me aside? Why do I follow the man who flees me? Why do I love the man who hates me? Ah, Flamminio! You have eyes only for Isabella. He wants no one but Isabella! He can have her. Take her! For I'll either leave him or die. I've decided no longer to serve him in these clothes and never to cross his path again so that he won't ever have to see the woman he finds so hateful. I'll go find Clemenzia. She's waiting for me at home. Together we'll plan what to do with my life.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: And if it's true, you can have me hung by the neck if cutting my tongue out isn't enough. That's what happened.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: When did it happen?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: When you sent me to look for him.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How? Tell me again, because he told me he didn't get to talk with her today.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: It would be better if he confessed. But I'll tell you that while I was waiting to see if he would show up at her house, I saw him come out. And as he was about to leave, Isabella called him back inside the doorway and then, after looking around to see if there was anyone to see them, not seeing anyone, they kissed each other.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How come they didn't see you, then?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Because I was hidden in that portico across the way, and they couldn't see me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How did you see them, then?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: With my eyes. Do you think that I saw them with my elbows?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: And he kisses her?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I don't know if she kissed him or he her, but I believe they kissed each other.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Did they each put their faces so close together that they could kiss?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Their faces no, but their lips yes.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Aha! Can two people bring their lips close without doing the same with their faces?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: All right, I suppose if people had their mouths in their ears or in the back of their necks it would be possible, maybe, but given where they are now, you're right.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Look, you'd better have seen things, because later you can't say, "Well, it seemed to me." This is a very serious thing that you're saying.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: As great as the giant Mangia, who rings the clock on the tower of Siena.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How did you see it?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Looking, with my eyes wide open, and as I was there to look, I really didn't have anything else to do but see.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: If this is true, you've killed me!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: It's true. She called him. They came together. She embraced him. She kissed him. So now if you want to die, go ahead.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I'm not surprised that the traitor denied being there! Now I understand why the rogue encouraged me to leave her - so that he could have her for himself! I won't deserve to be called a man if I don't launch a vendetta against him that will stand for all time as an example to servants who betray their masters. But in the end, if I don't have better proof, I don't want to believe you. I know that you're not trustworthy and that you must hate his guts, so you're saying this to get me to get rid of him. But in the name of God who I hold dear, I'll make you tell me the truth or kill you! Tell me! Did you really see it?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: He kissed her?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: They kissed.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How many times?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Two times.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: In the entrance hall.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You're a rotten liar! A little while ago you said they were in the doorway.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I meant to say near the doorway.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Tell the truth!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Ouch, ouch! I'm beginning to be sorry I told you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Did it really happen?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Yes, sir. But I forgot:I have a witness.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Who is it?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Scatizza, Virginio's servant.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: He saw them too?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Just like me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: And if he doesn't confirm what you said?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Kill me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: And if he confirms it?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I'll have to kill two people?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Oh, my God, why?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Not you two; Isabella and Fabio.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: And then you should burn down that house with Pasquella and everyone in it.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Let's find Scatizza. If I don't pay them as they deserve... if I don't make people talk... if the whole city doesn't see... I'll have such a great revenge! ... That traitor! That's what trust gets you.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: This city seems completely changed since I was last here. Actually I was here only briefly with the delegation from Ancona, and we stayed at the Guicciardino. Still, we were here about six days. [To FABRIZIO] Do you recognize anything?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: It's like I've never seen it before.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
