sp.p: That makes sense. After all, you left when you were so young that it's no wonder. Wait, I recognize this street. That's the palace of the Rangoni, over there's the Grand Canal, and that church you see there at the head of the street is the cathedral. Have you ever heard the saying "Were you ever the pussy of Modena" or "You think you're the pussy of Modena"?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: A thousand times. Show it to me, please.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: See that statue above the door of the cathedral?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: That one?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Wow! That's a scream!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Now you understand.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I've also heard the saying "You're trying to lead the bear of Modena." What does that mean, and where's this bear?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: There are sayings of the antiqui de quibus nescitur oigo.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I really have the feeling, Professor, that this place is going to bring me good things.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: And it's going to bring me even better things, because I smell the sweet pefume that comes from a roast, and it's making me die of hunger.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Oh! Don't you know what Cantalicius said? "Dulcis amor patriae". And Cato: "Pugna pro patria" Hoc, in summa, there is not a sweeter thing than one's fatherland.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I believe that Trebbiano wine is much sweeter, Tutor. Boy, could I use a cup of that now! My back's broken from carrying this baggage.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: These streets seem newly paved. When I was here before they were all dirty and muddy.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Are we going to stand around and count the cobblestones? Let's get going! Let's hurry up and find a place where we can eat, that's what I want.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Landundun animus est in patinis.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Whose coat of arms is that over there with the auger on it?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That's the coat of arms this community, and it's called the Trivella. And just as in Florence they cry "Marzocco, Marzocco!" and in Venice "San Marco, San Marco!" and in Siena "Lupa, Lupa!" here they cry "Trivella, Trivella!"

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I would rather we yell "Frying pan, frying pan!"

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: That one I recognize: it's the arms of the duke.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Tutor, why don't you carry this baggage yourself for a bit? My lips are so parched with thirst that I can barely talk.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Buck up. You can quench your first later!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: When I'm dead, then you'll make me a heavenly broth to drink.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I'm glad that I really like this place, event at first sight. What about you, Stragualcia?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: It seems like heaven to me: here too one doesn't eat or drink. Let's get going and not waste any more time looking at the place. We can look at it at our leisure after we eat.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: There you see the most egregious bell tower that exists in the whole structure of the universe.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Is that the one the people of Modena wanted to put a sheath over and whose shadow they claim makes a man go crazy?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes, that's it.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I know that as far as I'm concerned I'm not going to leave the kitchen. Whoever wants to wander around can do so. Now let's find a place to stay.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: You're in a great rush.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: A pox on you! Here I am dying of hunger, and I haven't had a thing to eat this morning besides that half a hen that you left me on the boat.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Whom can we find to show us to my father's house?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Actually, it seems to me that first we should find a place to stay at an inn and rest a bit there. Then we can look for him at our leisure,

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I like that idea. These seem to be inns.

div2.head: SCENE II
div2.stage: AGIATO, FRULLA, the PEDANT, FABRIZIO, and STRAGUALCIA

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Oh, kind sirs! This is the inn for you, if you want lodging. Come to the Mirror, to the Mirror!

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Oh, you're most welcome here! I've been your host other times. Don't remember your Frulla? Come in here, where all people of your quality put up.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Come stay with me. You'll have good rooms, a good fire, excellent beds, freshly washed sheets, and you'll not lack for anything that's yours.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I should certainly hope so!

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: I meant to say you won't lack for anything that's your desire.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: I'll give you the best wine in Lombardy, big fat birds, sausages like this, pigeons, large chickens, and whatever you ask for. And you'll really enjoy everything.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: This is what I want most of all.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: And you, what do you say?

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: I'll give you sweetbreads, mortadella, wine from the mountains, and above all you'll enjoy fine, delicate things.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: I'll give you lots of food, and you can forget delicate things. If you stay with me I'll treat you like lords, and you can pay me as you wish. At the Mirror, however, you'll pay for everything, even the candles. You decide.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Master, let's stay here, it's clearly better.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: If you want to lodge well, it would be better for you to stay with me. Do you want people saying that you're staying at the Joker?

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: My Joker is a hundred times better than your Mirror.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Speculum prudentia significat iuxia illud Catonis, "Nosce teipsum. " Do you understand, Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: See for yourself who has more guests, [tauntingly to AGIATO] you or me.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: See for yourself where the important people stay.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: See where they are better treated.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: See who has more fine things.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Enough of these fine things, fine things, fine things. I want just one thing, to fill my whole body, and you can keep your fine things, as far as I'm concerned. Too many fine things are fine for the Florentines.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: They all stay with me.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: They used to stay with you, but over the last three years they've all come over to my sign.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Young man, pit that baggage down here, for I see that it's tiring you out.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Don't worry about that, I've no desire to lighten the load on my shoulders until I'm sure I'm going to load up my belly.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Would a couple of fat capons do the trick? Bring the bag over here, and these are all yours.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Well, why not! But they'll only be an appetizer!

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Look at this prosciutto! Doesn't it look like crimson silk?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That's not bad.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Who knows about wine?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Me, me! Why, I know more than the French.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: See if you like this, then. If not, I can give you at least ten others.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Frulla, for my money you are a much better innkeeper than he is. He's not it backwards: he shows you something that will make you want to drink before he lets you see whether the wine is any good. [Tasting the wine] Oh, Master, this is good. Go ahead, take the bag.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Wait a moment. You, what do you have to say?

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: I say that gentlemen don't worry about stuffing their stomachs with a lot of food but rather eat small helpings of food that is fine and delicate.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: He must be running a hospital or an inn for the ill.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [To AGIATO] You're making sense. What will you give us?

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Ask for what you wish.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: I'm amazed at you gentlemen. When there is plenty of food, a man may eat as much or as little as he likes, which is not the case when there is little. Moreover, when a man begins to eat, his appetite grows and he needs to fill up with bread.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: "You are wiser than the law," as they say. I've never met a man who understands my needs better than you. Let's go, because I think I love you.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Go on into the kitchen, brother, and take a look around.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Omnis repletio mala, panis autem pessima.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Learned fool! One of these days I'll rearrange your teeth, if I live long enough.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Come with me, gentlemen, for it's not a prudent thing to stand around outside in the cold.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Oh, come now, we're not that fine and delicate!

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Listen, my lords, than inn in Lombardy. But ever since I opened the Joker, he's lucky if ten people stay there in a year. And my inn is better known than any other in the whole world. Lots of Frenchmen come here, and all the Germans who come through town.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: You're lying. The Germans go to the Pig.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Visitors from Milan, Parma, and Piacenza stay with me.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: The Venetians, Genoese, and Florentines stay with me.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Where do the Neapolitans stay?

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: With me.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Are you kidding? Most of them stay at the Love.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: And how many of them stay with me?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: The duke of Malfi, where does he stay?

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Sometimes with me, sometimes with him, sometimes at the Sword, sometimes at the Love, depending on what he wants.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Where do the Romans stay? Because we have come from Rome.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: With me.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: That's a lie. You won't find one who has stayed there all year. It's true that some old cardinals out of habit have stayed there, but all the new ones belong at the Joker.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [Coming out of the JOKER] I won't leave this place unless I'm dragged out. The others can go where they like. Master, there are so many big pots around the fire, so many soups, so many savories, so many sauces, such great spits of roasted pigeon, partridge, thrush, and goat, capons, boiled meats, roasts, and wonderful macaroni, lasagna, pies - if he were getting ready for carnival or the entire court of Rome, he would still have enough to satisfy everyone.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Did you try the wine?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: And that wine!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Variorum ciborum commistio pessima generat digestionem.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Bus asinorum, buorum castronorum, tatte, battate, pecoronibus! What the devil are you up to? May you catch the pox, you and all the other pedants in the world! You're a scoundrel, as far as I'm concerned. Let's stay here, Master.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Where do the Spanish stay?

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: I avoid having any dealings with them. They stay at the Bandit. But what else could you want? There isn't anyone who comes through here who doesn't stay with me, except for the Sienese, who are so friendly with the Modenese that when they visit they have a hundred friends who put them up in their homes. Lords and great professors, poor and rich, soldiers and good men, they all run to the Joker.

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: All the doctors, judges, friars, and learned men come to my inn.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: And I'll tell that there hardly passes a day that someone doesn't leave the Mirror to come and stay with me.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Tutor, what should we do?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Etiam atque etiam cogitandum.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Body of mine, it's time to fatten up. For once I'm going to eat my fill and rally pig out.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: I am thinking, Fabrizio, that we are rather low on funds.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Tutor, inside there I saw the innkeeper's young son, handsome as an angel.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Come on, then! Let's stay at the Joker. In any case, your father, if we find him, will pay the innkeeper.

p.seg: I thought that bit about the boy would be just the bait to catch that old bird! I've already had three glasses of wine, although I'm claiming only one. And I'm not going to leave the kitchen until I've tasted everything. Then I'll have a nap by that good fire. And to heel with anyone who wants to hold back!

sp.speaker: AGIATO:
sp.p: Watch out, Frulla. You've cheated me once too often, and one of these days we're going to have it out once and for all.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: Whenever you like. I'm ready and waiting.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Is this the way you've taught her to behave? Is this the honor she pays me? Oh, how unlucky I am! I've worked so hard to overcome my evil fortune, and for this? To see my patrimony without heirs; to see my house ruined; to see my daughter a whore; to become the subject of common gossip; to be unable to show my face in public; to be pointed out by children in the streets; to be help up as a warning by the old; to be put in a comedy by the Intronati; to be made an example of in tales; and to be made the subject of the gossip of every woman in this city? Maybe these women aren't gossips, eh? Maybe they don't like to malign others, eh? But I imagine it doesn't really matter, because everyone knows everything already. Actually, I'm certain, for if even one woman knows it, in three hours the whole town knows it. I'm a disgraced father, a miserable and sad old man who has lived too long! What can I do? What should I think?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You'd be better off making less noise so you can concentrate on making sure she returns home before the whole town finds out. But I think Sister Blabbermouth is as full of hot air as is the idea that Lelia is really running around town dressed as a man! Be sure that the nuns aren't just saying this because they hope you'll make her a nun and leave everything to the convent.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: How could she be lying? She even told me that Lelia is a servant of a Modenese gentleman and that he hasn't realized she's a woman.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Anything is possible, but me, I can't believe it.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: And I certainly can't believe he hasn't figured out that she's a woman.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I didn't mean that.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I have to say it, because my honor's on the line. Actually, I created the problem myself by giving the girl on to you to bring up even though I knew what you were.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Virginio, enough of such talk. If I've been a sinner, it's because you made me one. You know very well that before you, there was no one but my husband. And young girls need to be treated differently than you have treated Lelia. Aren't you ashamed to be trying to marry her off to a croaking old fool who could be her grandfather?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What do you have against old men, you slut? They're a thousand times better than young ones.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You've lost your senses, and that's why everyone is deceiving you and telling you such foolish gossip.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: If I find her, I'll drag her home by the hair.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: That way you'll belike those men who flaunt the horns on their own heads instead of sensibility hiding them.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I don't care. People will fins out anyway. The best that I can do is chop them off.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Do what think best, just be sure you don't chop off your head along with the horns.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I've been told how she's dressed, so I'm going to find her, and when I do there'll be hell to pay.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Do as you please. For myself, I'm off; no sense preaching to the deaf. These men!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: While my two servants are sleeping, I'm going to visit the town. When they wake up, tell them to head towards the main square.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: You know, my lord, if I hadn't seen you dressed in those clothes, I'd swear that you were the young servant of a local gentleman who dressed like you, in white, and is the spitting image of you.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Might he be some brother of mine?

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: He could.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Tell the Professor to find the person we've come to see me.

sp.speaker: FRULLA:
sp.p: I'll take care of it.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: My goodness, here he is. I was afraid I was going to have to search the whole city for him. Fabio, how good to see you! I was looking for you, so you've saved me the time and effort of finding you. My dear, my mistress wants you to come to see her right now about something of importance to you and her - I don't know what.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Who is your mistress?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You know very well who she is, you. My goodness, you two make a fine couple!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Actually, we're not a couple! But if she wants to couple, I'm ready.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I mean that you two aren't very quick. I'd like to be still young like you and able to enjoy such a feast! And I know that if I were you, I'd have already put aside my suspicions and scruples. But you'll get down to it soon enough, right?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Please, madam! You don't know me. You've mistaken me for someone else, so leave me alone.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, don't get me wrong, dear Fabio, I'm saying this to help you out.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I haven't gotten anything wrong. But my name isn't Fabio, and I'm not who you think.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Well, you two will have to work things out to your own satisfaction. But you know, there are very few young women her equal in wealth or beauty in this city. And I'd rather see you get down to it instead of running back and forth all the time, giving others reason to talk without gaining anything for yourself and with little honor for her.

p.seg: What's all this about? I don't understand. Either she's mad or she has mistaken me for someone else. But I want to see where she's leading me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh! I think I hear people in the house. Wait here a bit until I see if Isabella is alone. I'll call you if no one's there.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I want to see how this story ends. Maybe this woman is the servant of some courtesan and she thinks she'll get some money out of me. If that's the case, she's mistaken. I'm virtually a studen of the Spanish, and in the end I'll be more likely to have a scudo of hers before she has a carlin of mine. One of us will be deceived, and it won't be me. I'm going to move away a bit from this house so that I can see the type of people who go in and out and judge what type of person this woman is.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Please forgive me, but if that's what's happened, I'm going to turn her down. I'm afraid that your daughter did this because she didn't want me, and worse yet I'm convinced that she did it because she has had other lovers.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Don't think that, Gherardo. Do you think I would have told you any of this if that were the case? Please don't ruin our arrangements.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Please don't talk to me about it anymore.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Oh! Are you going to betray your word?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Yes, if someone's deeds betray me, I see no reason to keep my word. In the end you don't even know if you can get her back. You're trying to sell me the proverbial bird in the bush. Look, I heard everything you said to Clemenzia.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: As long as I don't have her, I won't try to give her to you, but if I get her back, wouldn't you be willing to marry her immediately?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Virginio, I had the most honorable wife who ever lived in this city, and I have a young daughter who's a pure dove. How can you ask me to take into my home a woman who has fled from her father and goes from house to house like a whore dressed as a man? Don't you understand that if I do that I won't be able to marry my daughter off?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: After a few days no one will be talking about it anymore. What does it really matter? And no one else besides us knows about it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Soon everyone in town will be talking.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: That's no true.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: How long has she been gone?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Since yesterday or this morning.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I wish to God it were true. But are you sure she's in Modena?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: All right. Find her, and then we can speak again.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Promise that you'll take her?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'll think about it.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Go ahead, say yes.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I can't say that, but...

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Go ahead, speak up.

p.seg: Quiet!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What do you think? She's busy praying before her little altar.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: May she be blessed! I have a daughter who's always praying. Who could ask for more?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, you've described her perfectly. She goes without meat every day that God requires it, and she says her prayers like a little saint.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: She's just like her blessed mother.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Exactly. Oh, the good that wretched woman did! She punished herself more and wore more hair-shirts than anyone else in recent history, and she made charity her life; and if it weren't for her love of you there wouldn't have been a friar, priest, or poor man who came to her door who wouldn't have received everything she had to offer.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Now those were good deeds!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Why, many times she'd get up an hour or two before dawn to go to the first mass of the Friars of Saint Francis, for she didn't want to be seen or thought to be a paud like certain saint sniffers I know.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What? "Badw"? What do you mean?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: That's right, "bawd." How do you say it?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: That's an insult!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I know I've heard her say it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You meant to say "fraud".

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Maybe. But what I really wanted to say is that her daughter is even more like that than she was.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Good willing.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [Seeing GHERARDO] Oh, Gherardo, Gherardo! Here's the person we were talking about! Oh, unhappy father that I am. She may hide or run, now that she's seen me. Grab her!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Be sure you're not making a mistake. Maybe it's not her.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Who wouldn't know her? Don't I see all the signs that Sister Blabbermouth told me to look for?

p.seg: Things are looking bad. I'm afraid I'm in trouble.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To FABRIZIO] Good day, young lady. Is this any way for a young lady to dress? Is this the way you honor your family? Is this the happiness you give to this poor old man? If only I'd been dead when I fathered you! It seems that the only reason you were born was to dishonor me and bury me alive! Oh, Gherardo! What do you think of your bride? Do you think she is bringing honor to us?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I wouldn't say so. My bride, hardly!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Tramp! Disgrace! It would serve you right if this man didn't want you as his wife any longer and no one else would take you! But he won't hold your foolishness against you; he wants to have you.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Not so fast!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [Pointing to GHERARDO’s house] Get in that house over there, you disgrace! It's clear that the milk your mother gave you the day that I sired you was damned.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Old man, don't you have sons, relatives, or friends in this city who can take care of you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What a reply! What are you talking about?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Well, in view of your need of a doctor, I'm amazed that they've let you out of the house. In any other city they'd keep someone like you tied down.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I ought to have kept you tied up! Why, I'd like to cut your throat! Bring me a knife.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Old man, you don't know mw very well. And perhaps you're insulting me like this because you think I'm a foreigner. But I'm as much from Modena as you and the son of a good a father and family as you yourself.

p.seg: She really is pretty. If there's no other problem than what one can see, I'll take her.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Well, then, why did you run off from your father and the place where I sent you?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: You never sent me anywhere that I know, but I was forced to leave.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Forced, eh? Who forced you?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: The Spaniards.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: And now where have you come from?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: From the military camp.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: From the military camp?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Yes, from the military camp.

p.seg: If that's how it is, the marriage is off!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You're ruined!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: And you too, old man!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Gherardo, please put her in your house so that she won't be seen in this state.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I will not. Send her to your own house!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: In the name of our friendship, let her in!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I said no.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Listen a second. [He and GHERARDO move off to talk privately] This way you'll be sure she won't run off.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: [Alone] I've known many crazies from Modena, whom I'll not name, but I've never seen any like this old man who weren't tied down or locked up. What a strange humor he's in! He's out of his mind, at least from what I can tell, because he seems to think that young men are young women. Oh, this is even more intriguingly strange than the story Molza told about a Sienese woman who thought she had become a Cretan vase, especially since women are usually held to be more foolish than old men, who for a host of reasons ought to be very wise. And not for a hundred scudi would I want to miss the chance to tell the tale of this madness during the carnival! But they're coming back. Let's see what they have to say.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'll tell you the truth, on the one hand I think I will, on the other I think I won't. Perhaps you could question her a little more closely.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To FABRIZIO] Come here.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: What do you want, old man?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You are a real sad case, you.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Don't insult me. I won't accept such treatment.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You disgrace!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Let him speak. Can't you see that he0s all worked up? Do as he says.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: What does he want from me? What do I have to do with you or him?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You still have the nerve to speak? Tell me, who is your father, eh?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I'll tell you: Virginio Bellenzini.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I wish to God it weren't true! You're going to make me die before my time.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: An old man of sixty dying before his time? Everyone should live so long! Why, you can go ahead and die anytime you like; you seem to have lived too long already.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: It’s all your fault, you tramp.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [To FABRIZIO] Enough of such talk, my little daughter, my dear sister. You shouldn't talk that way to your father.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: That's it - the madmen are joining ranks. Both of them seem to be suffering from the same delusion. [Laughing] What a strange case!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: How can you still laugh?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: It's a bad sign that you make fun of your own father.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: What father, what mother? I've never had another father than Virginio or another mother than Giovanna. You seem to be off your ricker. WHat do you think, that I have no father?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Going off again to talk privately with VIRGINIO] Virginio, you know what? I'm afraid that melancholy has caused this poor young woman to lose her mind.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Alas! I suspected it right away when she began treating me so aggressively.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Actually, that could be another reason.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: When a woman has lost her honor, she thinks the whole world is hers and becomes aggressive.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: She seems merely crazy to me.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Still, it's strange that she remembers her father and mother yet doesn't seem to recognize you.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Let's make her go into your house; it's right here. We can't get her to mine without alerting the whole city.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: [Aside] What are these two senile brothers of ancient Melchizedek plotting now?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Let’s try to lure her into the house with kindness and then lock her up with your daughter in her room.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: All right, let’s try.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [Coming back with GHERARDO to speak with FABRIZIO] Look here, my daughter, I don’t want to stay angry with you. I’ll forgive everything if you’ll try to be good.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Now that’s the way good daughters behave.

p.seg: Now the other one’s cooked.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Look here, it’s not honorable to be seen talking out here dressed up like that. Come into the house. Pasquella, open the door!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Go in, my daughter.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: I’m certainly not going to do that.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Because I don’t like entering the houses of strangers.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'm blessed! She'll be a perfect wife, like Penelope!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Didn't I tell you that my daughter was beautiful and good?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Her manners show through.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To FABRIZIO] I only want to have a word with you.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: You can have it out here.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: No, out here is not the place! This house is yours because you’re going to be my wife.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: What wife? Why, you old bugg— ... you humbugger!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Your father has betrothed you to me.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: What are you thinking? Do you think I’m one of those pansy boys that you can ... eh?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To GHERARDO] Come on! Don’t get her all upset. [To FABRIZIO] Listen, my child. I don’t want to do anything that you don’t want.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: Look, old man, you’re mistaken about me.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Just a few words inside.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: [Going in the house] As many as you like. Do you think I'm afraid of you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Gherardo, now that you have her inside let's have her locked up with your daughter in her room until we can send for her clothes.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: As you wish, Virginio. Pasquella, bring the key to Isabella's room and call Isabella.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: It would serve you right if he gave you a good beating to teach you that when he goes out, you should go with him instead of getting drunk and then sleeping it off.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: And he ought to load you up with kindling, sulfur, pitch, and gunpowder and then set you alight to teach you not to be what you are.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Drunkard! Drunkard!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Pedant! Pedant!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Wait till I find our master!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Wait till I find his father!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Oh! What do you want to tell his father about me?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: And you, what can you say about me?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That you're a fool, a crook, a fraud, a thug, a madman, a drunkard!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: And I can say that you're a thief, a gambler, a gossip, a cheat, a swindler, an impostor, a braggart, a fathead, a disgrace, an ignoramus, a traitor, a sodomite, and an evil person!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: It seems we've met.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Enough. I don't want to get mixed up with your sort; there's no honor in it for me.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Yes, by God! One finds in you all the nobility of the Maremma. Will you ever be anything but the son of a mule driver? Aren't I from a better family than you? Is it right that this fool should lord it over everybody just because he knows how to say cuius masculini.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Alas! "Poor and nude, philosophy journeys through this world." Latin has come on hard times when it comes form the mouth of an ass.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: The ass will be you, and I'll give you a good beating if you don't change your tune.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: You should remember the proverb "Furor sit laesa saepius sapientia." You're about to make me lose my temper, Stragualcia. Back off, you big ugly manure shoveler, you villain, you archvillain!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Hey! Pedant, archpedant, pedant, greatest pedant! Is there any insult worse than "pedant"? Is there a worse type? Is there a greater fraud? Is there a worse profession? Maybe it wouldn't be so bad if they didn't go around all puffed up because others call them "Messer So and So" or "Professor Such and Such," or if they deigned to respond to someone who doffs his hat to them before they're a mile past. "Good day to you, Sir Crap, Sir Turd. Professor Diarrhea, Sir Shit!"

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Tratant fabrilia fabri. You're talking about exactly what you are.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I'm talking about what you like.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Could you get your ass out of my way?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I would never let my ass be in your way, although I imagine you would like to have had it in your way.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: By the body of- ...

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: By the body of- ... You'd better watch out if you're going you to start swearing at me [Aside, but said so that the PEDANT can overhear] He ought to realize that I know about all his evil deeds and that if I wanted to, I could have him burned. Yet he still insists on busting my ass.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: You're lying! I'm not that kind of man.

p.seg: He would be one of the first pedant who wasn't.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: I've decided, Stragualcia, that this house is not big enough for both of us.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Hoy original! Is this the first time I've heard you say this? Look, you aren't about to leave unless someone chases you out the door with you, to give you a place to sleep, if not this young man who's as good as they come?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: For God's sake, as if I couldn't find another post if I wanted to. Why, there's even someone who made me an excellent offer.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Come on, come on, do you expect me to believe that crap?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Enough, and you would be wise to keep quiet. Now go back to the inn and look after our master's things. We can settle this later.

p.seg: If I didn't threaten this bugger every now and then, I couldn't live with him. He's lower than a rabbit. When I threaten him, he keeps quiet, but if I let him get on top of me he'd do his worst, given his tastes! It's a good thing I know his character.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [Alone] Frulla told me that Fabrizio will be someplace around the central square. I'd better get going.

div2.head: SCENE II

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: As far as the dowry is concerned, what we agreed to is agreed to. I'll give her the dowry you asked for, and you'll add a thousand florins if you don't find your son.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: That's fine.

p.seg: If I'm not mistaken, I've seen this gentleman before. But I don't remember where.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To the PEDANT] What are you staring at, my good man?

p.seg: Clearly this is my master.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Let him stare at whatever he wishes. He seems to be a stranger here, and as you know, in other places they don't even think twice about staring at anyone they want to.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: If I stare, it's not sine causa. Tell me, do you know a Messer Virginio Bellenzini who lives in this city?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Yes, I know him. Actully, I have no closer friend. But what do you want with him? If you're thinking of staying with him, I should tell you that he's busy with other things and he can't put you up. You'd wise to find other lodgings.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: You are clearly he. Salvete, patronorum optime!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Could you possibly be Messer Pietro de'Pagliaricci, my son's tutor?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes, it is I.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [Beginning to weep] Oh, my son! Alas! What news do you have of him? Where did you leave him? Where did he die? Why did you wait so long to contact me? Did those traitors, those Jews, those dogs kill him? My poor son! He was the only good I had in the world. O my dear Professor, tell me immediately, please!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Don't cry, sir, please.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: O Gherardo, my son-in-law, here's the man who taught my poor son while he was alive. O Professor! O my son! Where are you buried? Don't you know? Why don't you tell me? I'm dying to know, and I'm dying of fear that I'll learn what I don't want to.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Oh, don't cry, Master. Why are you crying?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Shouldn't I cry for such a sweet son? So wise, so learned, so well brought up! And those traitors, they've taken him away from me, killed him.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: May God keep you both well, you and him. Your son is alive and well.

p.seg: I'm the loser, if this is true. I'm out a thousand florins.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Alive and well? If that were true, he would be with you now.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Virginio, do you know this fellow well? Could this be some kind of trick?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Parcius ista viris, tamen obiicienda memento.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Explain, Professor.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Your son was taken prisoner by a certain Captain Orteca during the sack of Rome.

p.seg: Oh boy, now the story begins.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: And because the captain captured him along with two others, he decided to trick them by secretly sending your son and me to Siena. But a few days later he began to worry that those gentlemen of Siena -who are great lovers of law and fair play and friends of our city and above all else good men- would free your son. So he moved him from Siena to a castle of the lord of Piombino. In the meantime he made us write per usque millies asking for the ransom he had set of one thousand ducats.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: My poor son! Did they torture him as well?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: No, in fact they treated him like a gentleman.

p.seg: I'm afraid I can see what's coming.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: We never had any reply to the letters we sent.

p.seg: You understand that this is the way he intends to get his hands on your money.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [To the PEDANT] Go on.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Then the Spaniard took us with him on campaign in Correggio, where he was killed. After that the court took control of his property, and we were freed.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Where is my son, then?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Closer that you think.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: In Modena?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: If you promise me some refreshment, quia omnis labor optat praemium, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: This is what he's after, the fraud!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [To GHERARDO] You're mistaken. I, a fraud? Absit!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I'll promise you anything you want. Where is he?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: At the inn of the Joker.

p.seg: It's done: the thousand ducats are played and lost. But what does it matter to me? As long as I have Lelia, I'm fine. I'm rich enough as it is.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Let's go, Professor. I can't wait to see him and embrace him and kiss him and hold him in my arms!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Master, oh, quanto mutatus ab illo! He's no longer a child to hold in your arms. You wouldn't recognize him. He's grown up, and I'm sure he won't recognize you either, what with how much you've changed. Praeterrea, you have the beard now which you didn't have before, and if I hadn't heard your voice I wouldn't have recognized you. And Lelia, how is she?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Well. She's all grown up and rounded out.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Rounded out? You mean she's pregnant? If that's the case, you can keep her! I don't want her.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Oh no! Oh no! I mean she's become grown, shapely woman. Oh, Tutor, I haven't embraced you yet.

div2.stage: [He takes the PEDANT in his arms and kissed him on both cheeks]

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Master, not that I want to brag, but the things I have done for your son -I could tell you! And in turn there was never a thing I asked of him that he didn't do immediately.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: How did his studies go?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: He didn't lose any time, ut licuit per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Call him out here, but don't tell him anything. I want to see if he recognizes me.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: He left the inn a little while ago. Let's see if he has returned.

div2.head: SCENE III
div2.stage: The PEDANT, STRAGUALCIA, VIRGINIO, and GHERARDO

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Stragualcia! Oh, Stragualcia! Has Fabrizio returned?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Not yet.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Come here. Say something to my oId master. This is Messer Virginio.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [To the PEDANT] Are you still angry?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Don't you know that I never stay angry with you?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Now give your hand to Fabrizio's father.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [To the PEDANT] You should give me your hand.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Not to me, to this gentleman.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Is this our master's father?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [Giving VIRGINIO his hand] O magnificent Master, you are just in time to pay the innkeeper. Welcome!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: This man was a good servant to your son.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Are you suggesting that I won't be in the future?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You are most welcome, my son! I think I ought to reward all those who have given my son such support.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: You can reward me with a very little thing.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Tell me what.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Get me a job as a servant with this innkeeper, who's the greatest guy in the world and the best supplied and the wisest and the one who best understands a traveler's needs of any innkeeper I've ever met. As far as I'm concerned, this is paradise.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: He has an excellent reputation as a host.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Have you eaten?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: A little.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What have you had?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: A couple of partridges, six thrushes, a capon, a bit of veal, and only two tankards of wine.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Frulla, give him what he wants and leave the bill to me.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Now are you happy?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [With a Spanish accent] Let me kiss your hands. This is the way masters should be! Tutor, you're too cheap and want everything for yourself. How many people have told you that? Frulla, bring these gentlemen something to drink.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That's not necessary.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I know you'll drink. I'll pay. It's no big deal. Some sweet-breads, a slice of salami ... won't you have some? Tutor, come on, have something to drink.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: All right, to make peace with you.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Oh, he's good, Master. You should love the Tutor, for he loves your son more than his own eyes.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: May God reward him!

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: First it's your turn, then God's. [To GHERARDO] And you, sir, have some wine.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I really shouldn't.

div2.stage: [Accepts a glass of wine and takes a sip]

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Please, come on in until Fabrizio returns, and then, since dinner is all ready, let's eat here this evening.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: That's not a bad idea.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'll leave you, as I have a little matter to take care of at home.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Be careful that she doesn't get away.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: That's exactly why I'm going home.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: She's all yours, now. Take care of things as you see fit. As far as I'm concerned, you can do as you please.

div2.stage: [He and the others go into the inn as GHERARDO heads towards his house]

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Alone] In the end one can't have everything. Patience! [Looking offstage] But if I'm seeing clearly, that's Lelia, who has somehow escaped! That silly servant girl has let her get away!

div2.head: SCENE IV
div2.stage: LELIA (dressed as a boy), CLEMENZIA, and GHERARDO

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: [As GHERARDO approaches, unseen] Don't you think, Clemenzia, that Fortune enjoys toying with me?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Relax and leave it to me. I'll find some way to make it all work out for you. But go and change those clothes before you're seen like that.

p.seg: I want both to greet her and to find out how she escaped.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: [To GHERARDO] Who are you speaking to? What Lelia? I'm not Lelia.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh! Didn't your father and I lock you up with my daughter Isabella a few minutes ago, and didn’t you admit that you were Lelia? And do you think I wouldn't recognize my own wife? Go and change those clothes.

sp.speaker: LELIA:
sp.p: [As she enters CLEMENZIA'S house] You're crazy if you think I'd want a husband!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You go home too, my dear Gherardo. All women are a bit strange, some in one way, some in another. And you should know that there are very few, in fact probably none, who don't do something a little offbeat now and then. Such things, however, are best kept secret.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: As far as I'm concerned, it will remain a secret. But how did she get out of my house? I had locked her up with Isabella.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Who? Her?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Her.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You're deceiving yourself! She's been with me the whole day. And in a playful moment she decided to put on these clothes and asked me if they suited her, as young girls sometimes do.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Are you trying to kid me? I'm telling you, we put her in my house with Isabella!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Where are you coming from now, then?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: From the inn of the Joker, where I went with Virginio.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Did you drink anything?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Just a sip.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Well, go and sleep it off. You clearly need to.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Let me speak with Lelia a bit before I leave. I have some good news for her.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Her brother has returned safe and sound, and her father is waiting for him at the inn.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Who, Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Fabrizio.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: If it's true, I'll give you a kiss.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: How beautiful happiness is! But as far as the kiss is concerned, I would prefer to give it to Lelia.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I'm going to run and tell her.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: And I'm going to give hell to that imbecile who let her escape!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh dear! I had such a scare that I've run out of the house. [To the audience] Ladies, you won't believe what's happened if I don't tell you. So I will tell you, but not those dirty-minded men, who would just laugh. Those two old muttonheaded dolts were absolutely convinced that that young man was a woman, and they locked him up with my mistress, Isabella, in her bedroom and gave me the key. After a while I decided to go in to see what was up, and I found them hugging and kissing! So I decided to find out whether it was a man or a woman. My mistress had the person down on the bed, and she called me to help her while she held his hands. And he was letting her win, so I opened the front of his clothes, and all of a sudden I felt something slap my hand, and I wasn't sure whether it was a large pestle or a big stick or that other thing. But whatever it was, it was in great shape. And when I saw how big it was, I took off, sisters, and locked the door behind me! And I can tell you that as far as I'm concerned, I have no intention of going back in there alone. And if one of you ladies doesn't believe me and wants to see for herself, I'll lend her the key. But here comes Giglio. I want to see if I can get that rosary and make a fool of him; these Spaniards think so much of themselves that they don't believe there's anyone else in the world as clever as they are.

div2.head: SCENE VI

p.seg: There's Pasquella. I bet she's been getting herself pretty worked up, waiting so long for me. She already know, the slut, how good we Spaniards are with women. Oh, these Italian whores really get off on us!
I've already figured out how to deceive this guy. Leave it to me.

This low-life washerwoman, she thinks I'll give her the rosary. The emperor be damned if I don't get her to love me so much that she buys me dozens of socks and shirts and jackets. I'll use her as I please, and afterwards I'll take off with my rosary without a word. Maybe she's already forgotten it.
If he lets me get my hands on that rosary just once, he'll never see it again or you can cut out my eyes. And if he complains, I'll have my Spela give him a beating like he's never had before.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: [To PASQUELLA] Oh, blessed is the mother who gave birth to such a beautiful woman, so well formed, so true! I think that you have been longing for me.

p.seg: What beautiful bull they dish out!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: My God, I am devastated that I was held up but other business. But let's go in now.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I'm afraid my master will return; he's been gone for a while. But you've forgotten the rosary, eh?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: No, madam. I have it here with me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Show me. Oh! You were going to fix it. Why haven't you?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I'll get it fixed later. To tell you the truth, it slipped my mind.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Well! I see how much I mean to you, womanizer that you are! I'd like to-

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: [Interrumping] Don't get angry, madam, with your son. You know I don't have any women friends other than you.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: It' hasn't taken me long to catch you in lie. A little while ago you said you had two gentlewomen for friends.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I gave them up for you. I don't want anyone else besides you. Don't you understand me?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: All right. But is that string of beads really a rosary? It seems pretty long to me.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I don't know how many beads there are.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: That's a sign that you don't say it very often. I'm beginning to wonder if you even know your Our Father. Oh well, give it to me for a second, and I'll count the beads.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Take it. [He hands it to her] But let's go into the house.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Should we? Take a look around to see if anyone would see you come in.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: [Looking around] There's no one around.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Let's go in. [Opening the door a crack] Oops, oh dear, my hens are all here at the door! Wait a second, Giglio. Move over there. If they get away it'll take all day to round them up.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Hurry up!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Back, back, my pretty ones, my pretty ones, shoo, shoo! May you break your necks! Some of them are getting away. Watch out, watch out, Giglio!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Where are these hens? From here I don't see any hens, or cocks for that matter.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You don't? They're over here. Move back a little and let me close the door for a bit so that I can put them back where they belong.

div2.stage: [She enters the house, closing and locking the door]

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Hey, you're locking the door! Why are you doing that?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Because I don't want any cocks opening it.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Hurry up before someone comes along and disturbs us.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: It doesn't matter who comes along, as no one is opening anything.

p.seg: Damn her, the old hag.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: My dear Giglio, don't you realize that first I must say this whole rosary? You can forget about this evening. And I forgot, I also have a prayer to say that I mustn't overlook.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Who foolishness is this? What rosary, what prayer?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What prayer? Do you want me to teach it to you? It's a good one: "Ghost, ghost, the wanders day and night, if you have come all hard to me, all hard you'll have to leave. Evil with evil, you've come to me at the wrong time thinking to have me, and you will remain deceived. Amen."

p.seg: In the name of all the holy martyrs, if this ugly old babbling untrustworthy bat has tricked me ...

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Singing] "What is my lover doing that he doesn't come? The love of another girl keeps him away from me." Alas!

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: What? Don't say that, my lady Pasquella! He's right here, waiting for you to let him in.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Singing] "I cannot serve you, my dear lord." Oh dear!

p.seg: More songs, that damn woman. She doesn't realize that I'm out there. I'll knock on the door, I swear to God.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Your little boy.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What do you want? My master's not at home. Do you want to leave a message?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: A word.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Wait a bit, he should be here shortly.

p.seg: May the whole world be damned if I don't burn down this house if she doesn't give me my rosary!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Pounding on the door] Hello! Who's there? Could you be a little more discreet? Forgive me, but who are you? Oh my! Are you trying to break down the door?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: I swear by God and event Saint Litany that I'll burn down this door if you don't give me back my rosary!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Maybe you should look elsewhere. We usually don't grow roses in our garden.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: You misunderstand, I'm saying my rosary beads, my Our Fathers.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What business is it of mine if you say your Our Fathers? Are you suggesting that I should become a false convert like you Spanish Jews, and that I'd need to learn them over again like you?

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Damn you, you whore, you old hag! Now you're calling me a false convert?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You know that? If you don't get away from that door, I'm going to throw water on you.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: Go ahead, throw your water. I'm going yo burn down your door. [PASQUELLA dumps a bucket of water on him] Damn you! She has drowned me, this woman, hag, old whore, tramp! To hell with all that's holy!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Did you get all wet? I didn't notice you. [GHERARDO enters] But here comes my master. If you want something, ask him and don't brother me anymore.

sp.speaker: GIGLIO:
sp.p: If that old man finds me here, I'll be in big trouble. I'd better get out of here.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What were you up to with that Spaniard here by the door? What do you have to do with him?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: He was asking about some rose garden. But I didn't pay any attention to him.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Well, you sure did exactly as I told you! I'd like to break your neck.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Why did you let Lelia escape? Didn't I tell you not to let her out?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What do you mean, escape? Isn't she in the room?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: God damn you!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I know she's there, I'm sure of it!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: And I know she isn't there, because I just left her in the house of her balia, Clemenzia.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Why, I just left her in the bedroom on her knees running through her Our Fathers with Isabella.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Maybe she got back before me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: I tell you, she never left. The room has been locked the whole time.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Where's the key?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Right here.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Give it to me. And if she's not there, I'll break your neck!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: And if she is there, will you give me a blouse?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Let me open the door.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Leaving with the key] No, I want to open it myself. You'd find some excuse.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh my! I hope he doesn't find them still going at it. But it's been a while since I left them.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: [Entering] Pasquella, how long ago did my Fabio leave?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Because he's a traitor, and I'm going to punish him. And because Isabella has left me for him, she'll get what she deserves, too. Oh, what a fine thing - for a noblewoman to fall in love with a mere serving boy!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, don't get all worked up! The caresses she gave him, she gave as a sign of her love for you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You can tell her that one day she'll be sorry. And you can tell him that when I find him (I have this knife in my hand for this), I plan to cut off his lips and ears and cut out one of his eyes and give them all to her on a plate. That way she can kiss them as much as she likes!

p.seg: That's how it goes! "While the dog barks, the wolf eats his fill."

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You just wait and see.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Entering in a rage] Oh, my God! Is this what things have come to? This is it, then? I'm ruined! That traitor Virginio! That dirty traitor! He's made an ass of me. Oh, God! What can I do?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What's wrong, Master?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What's wrong? Who is that man with my daughter?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, don't you know? Isn't it Virginio's baby girl?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Baby girl, eh? A baby girl that will make my daughter have babies of her own! Oh, how I'm suffering!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: My, don't say such things! What's wrong? Isn't it Lelia?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'm telling you, that's a man in there.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What? That can't be true. You can't be right!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I saw him with my own eyes.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: On top of my daughter, alas!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Oh, these kids today are great pranksters.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I wish it were a prank!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Are you sure it was a man?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Yes. I tell you, I opened the door suddenly and there he was with only his doublet on, and he didn't have time to cover himself.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You're sure you saw everything? Look, maybe it was a woman!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I tell you, it was a man, and he was well enough endowed to make two men.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: What did Isabella say?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What do you think she said? That I should be ashamed, maybe?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Why don't you let that young man go? What do you want to do with him?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: What can I do? Haul him before the courts and have him punished.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: But maybe he'll escape.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Impossible. I locked him back in. But there's Virginio. Just the man I'm looking for.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: I'm really surprised that he still hasn't returned to the inn. I don't know what to say.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Was he armed?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Then I'm afraid he may have been arrested for carrying arms. We have a Podesta who's a tough as nails.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: I don't think they would treat a foreigner so badly.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Entering] Good day to you, Virginio. Is this the way a gentleman acts? Is this the way to treat a friend? Is this the way you wanted to become my relative? Who did you think you were fooling with? Did you think I would accept this? I'd like to –

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: [Interrupting] Why are you upset with me, Gherardo? What have I done to you? I wasn't the one who wanted to become your relative; you've been nagging me about this for a year. Well, if you've changed your mind now, we can forget about it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Why, you have some nerve acting as if I was the one in the wrong! Dirty traitor, fraud, crook, swindler! But the courts will learn everything.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Gherardo, such language is not fitting for one of your station and even less so to use with me.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: He doesn't even want me to complain, this swine! You've become all haughty because your son has returned, eh?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: You're the swine.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, God! If I were young again, I'd cut you to pieces.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Would it be possible to find out what you're talking about?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You housewrecker!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I'm too patient with this man.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Thief!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Forger!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: You're lying. Just wait ...

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I'm waiting.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [Restraining GHERARDO, who takes off his vest and approaches VIRGINIO threateningly] Ah, my good man, why this madness?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Let me go!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Sir, put your vest back on.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Who do you think you're dealing with? Give me back my daughter.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: I'll cut both your throats!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Why is this gentleman so upset with you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I've no idea. Perhaps it has something to do with the fact that a little while ago we put my daughter Lelia in his house because he wanted to take her as his wife. Now you see how is. I'm afraid he might harm her.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [Seeing GHERARDO coming out of his house with a pike] Ah, ah, good sir! Let's not get started with weapons! No weapons!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Get out of my way!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: What is the problem?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: This traitor has ruined me.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: If I don't cut him to pieces, if I don't slice him into quarters with this pike ...

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: In God's name, please tell me what's wrong.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Let's go into my house and I'll explain, since that traitor has fled. Aren't you his son's tutor? Weren't you at the inn with us?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Come in.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: With faith in your word.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Oh, you can count on that!

div2.head: SCENE I
div2.stage: VIRGINIO [with a large shield and a mail shirt], STRAGUALCIA, SCATIZZA [with a small round shield], several of VIRGINIO's servants [with various makeshift weapons], GHERARDO, the PEDANT, and FABRIZIO

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: All of you, come with me. Stragualcia, you too.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: With weapons or without? I don't have any weapons.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Get some from the inn.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: You know, Master, with a large shield like that you should have a lance.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: I don't need a lance. This is enough for me.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: This small round shield would be more noble, since you're wearing a mail shirt.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: No, this covers me better. Oh! This muttonhead seems to think he's caught me trying to swindle him somehow. And I'm afraid he may have killed my poor daughter.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: [Coming out of the inn with a roast on a spit and a bottle of wine] This is a fine weapon, Master. I'm going to run this spit through him like a woodcock!

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Oh! But what are you going to do with the roast?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: I have military experience, and I know that the first thing you need to do is be sure you have field rations.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: And the wine, what's that for?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: To refresh the troops, if the first attrack is rebuffed.

sp.speaker: SCATIZZA:
sp.p: Sounds good to me, and it's likely.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Do you want me to run them all through - the old man, the daughter, the servants, the whole household and all of them, like chicken livers to be roasted? Why, I'll run this spit through side by side like thrushes.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: The door is open. They may have set some kind of ambush.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Bushes? That's bad. I'm more afraid of being with switches than swords. But the Tutor is coming out.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: [Coming out of the house and speaking to GHERARDO, who remains inside] Leave this to me, and I'll make peace for you, Messer Gherardo.

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Look at that, Master. It's the Tutor, and it seems that he has mutinied and gone over to the enemy. You can't count on his type to stay loyal! Do you want me to start with him, running him through so that I can say "one down"?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Messer Virginio, my master, why are you armed?

sp.speaker: STRAGUALCIA:
sp.p: Aha! Didn't I tell you!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: What has happened to my daughter? Hand her over. I want to take her home. And have you found Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Where is he?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: He's here inside. And he has taken a very beautiful bride, with your permission.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: A wife, eh? And who would that be?

p.seg: That was quick. This is rich, rich!

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: The beautiful and well-mannered daughter of Gherardo.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Oh! The same Gherardo who just now wanted to kill me?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Rem omnem a principia audies. Come on into the house, and you'll hear the whole story. Come on out, Messer Gherardo.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: [Coming out of the house] Oh, Virginio, this is the strangest case ever! Come in.

p.seg: Should I run him through? But his meat is hardly worth roasting.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Have your men put down their weapons. This is a matter for laughter.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Can I trust you?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Yes, certainly, on my word.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: All right, go on home everyone! And put down your weapons and bring me my vest.

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: Fabrizio, come out and meet your father.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: Oh! Isn't this Lelia?

sp.speaker: PEDANT:
sp.p: No, this is Fabrizio.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: O my dear son!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO:
sp.p: O my father, I've searched so long for you!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: O my dear son, I've cried so long for you!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO:
sp.p: Come in, come in, and you'll hear the whole story. And I should tell you also that your daughter is safe in the house of Clemenzia, her balia.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO:
sp.p: O dear God, how grateful I am to You!

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I saw him with these eyes and I heard him with these ears in the house of Clemenzia.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Are you sure it was Fabio?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Do you think that I don't know him?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Let's go. If I find him ...

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: You'll ruin everything. Be patient, and wait until he comes out.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Not even God could give me enough patience.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: You're going to ruin the cake.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I am going to ruin myself.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: A friend of yours. Come down to the door.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Oh! What do you want, Messer Flamminio?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Open the door and I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Wait a second until I come down.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: [To CRIVELLO] As soon as she opens the door, go in and see if he's there, then call me.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Leave it to me.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: [Opening the door] What do you want, Signor Flamminio?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What's my boy doing in your house?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What boy? [Blocking CRIVELLO as he tries to push past her into the house] And you, Crivello, where are you going, you rascal? Do you think you can enter my house by force?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Clemenzia, by the holy, inviolate, sacred body, if you don't hand over that ...

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What do you want me to hand over?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: My boy, who's hiding in your house.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: There's no serving-boy of yours in my house, even if there is a serving-girl

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Clemenzia, thi is not the time to fool around.You've always been a friend of mine. You've helped me out, and Iove helped you. But this is too important.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: This must be some madness induced by love. Calm down, Flamminio, cool down a bit.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I said, hand over Fabio.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I'll hand him over.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Enough! Make him come down here now.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Oh, calm down, for God's sake! You know, if I were young and you liked me, I wouldn't give you the time of day. By the way, how's Isabella?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I wish she were cut into pieces!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Hah! I don't believe you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You don't believe me? I can tell you that she's cleared things up for me just fine.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Really! Well, you young colts deserve every setback, because you are the most ungrateful people in the whole world.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You can't say that about me. Every other accusation might fit, but to be called ungrateful, no. There's not a man alive who dislikes such behavior more.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I'm not talking about you. But there was once here in this city a young girl who, realizing that she was admired by a knight – one of your peers here in Modena – fell so in love with him that she lost sight of everything else.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Lucky man! Happy man! I certainly couldn't say as much for myself.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: It so happened that her father sent this poor girl, so in love, away from Modena. Fearing that her lover would forget her, she cried so much that it was a wonder to see. And in fact he immediately found another girl, as if she had never existed.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I'd say that such a man should be called a traitor, not a knight.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Listen, it gets worse. When the young girl returned after several months, she found that her lover loved another who didn't love him. Abandoning her house and her father and putting her honor at risk, she decided to serve him. So she dressed herself as a young manservant and took a job with her lover as his servant.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: This is happened in Modena?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: And you know then both.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I would rather be this lucky lover than the lord of Milan.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Do you want to hear the rest? This lover of hers, not recognizing her, used her as his go-between with his new love. And to make him happy, this poor girl did everything he asked.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Oh, what a virtuous woman! What constant love! This love could serve as a lesson for future centuries. Why can't I be so lucky?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Well, you wouldn't give up Isabella for such a love anyway.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Why, I'd almost be willing to say I'd give up Christ for someone like that. Please, Clemenzia, tell me who this woman is.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: I'd be glad to. But first I want you to tell me, on your oath as a gentleman, what you would do with such a poor girl if such a thing happened to you. Would you kick her out when you learned what she'd done? Would you kill her, or would you judge her worthy of some reward?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I swear in the name of the power of the sun that you see in the sky, and with the proviso that I be banned forever from the company of my peers, gentlemen and knights, that I would take her as my wife – even if she were ugly; even if she were poor; even if she were of low birth; even over the daughter of the duke of Ferrara.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: That's a big oath. Are you ready to stand by it?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Yes, I'm saying it, and yes, I would do it.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: [Turning to CRIVELLO] You're a witness.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I heard him, and I know he would do it.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Now I want to introduce you to this woman and to this knight. Fabio, oh, Fabio! Come down here. Your master is looking for you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: What do you make of this, Crivello? Do you think I should kill this traitor? He's at least a good servant.

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: Oh well! I'm hardly surprised! I thought something strange like this would happen. Go ahead, pardon him. What else is there to do? That tart Isabella never really loved you anyway.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You're right.

div2.head: SCENE III
div2.stage: PASQUELLA, CLEMENZIA, FLAMMINIO, LELIA[dressed as a woman], and CRIVELLO

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Comming out of GHERARDO's house and speaking with someone inside] I'll take care of it. I'll tell him what you told me and what I've learned.

div2.stage: [LELIA comes to the door of CLEMENZIA's house where the others are standing]

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: This, Messer Flamminio, is your Fabio. Take a good look. Do you recognize him? Are you surprised? And this same girl is that young woman I told you about, so loyal and so true to her love. Take a good look, and see if you recognize her. Have you lost your voicie, Flamminio? Well, what do you have to say now? And you, you are that young man who thought so little of the love of his mistress. Don't think that you're the one of the deceived here! You can see for yourself that I'm telling the truth. Now keep your word, or I'll take you before the courts as someone who has broken his pledge.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: I don't believe there's ever been a more perfect deception than this one. How could I have been so blind that I never recognized her?

sp.speaker: CRIVELLO:
sp.p: I was more blind than anyone. I looked at her closely a thousand times and never realized. I'll be damned! Oh, whay a fool I've been!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: [Interrupting] Clemenzia, Virginio told me to tell you to come to our house right now because he has married off Fabrizio, his son who returned today. And he needs you to put the house in order, because, as you know, he has no other woman.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: What wife? Whom did he marry him to?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Isabella, the daughter of Gherardo, my master.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: Who? Isabella, the daughter of Gherardo Foiani, your master, or another Isabella?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Another? No, it's her. Flamminio, it's like they say: "Some people have all the luck.”

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: You're sure it's true?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Absolutely. I was there for the whole thing. I saw him give her the ring, and then they embraced, they kissed, and they rejoiced. And even before he gave her the ring she gave him ... well, let's just say, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: How long ago did this happen?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Now, just now. Then they sent me running here to tell Clemenzia and to bring her back.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Tell them I'll be there shortly. Go on, now.

p.seg: O God, You've made things come together so well! I'm dying of happiness.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Don't take too long, I've so much to do that I'm all in a dither! I need to go now to buy some makeup. Oh! I forgot to ask if Lelia's here, because Gherardo has agreed to marry her.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: You know very well that she's here. Do you really want to see her married to that poor old excuse for a man, your master? He ought to be ashamed of himself!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: You don't really know my master. Why, if you knew how manly he can be, you wouldn't talk about him like that.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Sure, sure, I believe you. I bet you've tested his manliness.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA:
sp.p: Just like you with your master. Anyway, I'm off.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
sp.p: She's to be married to Gherardo?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA:
sp.p: Yes, woe is me! Isn't this poor girl unlucky?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO:
